Log-concavity and Approximate Counting for Totally Unimodular Polytopes

Jonathan Leake    Maryam Mohammadi Yekta
September 2026
Abstract

We present a new lower bound on the number of lattice points of all totally unimodular polytopes, generalizing previous lower bounds on contingency tables, integer flows, and beyond. Our bound is based on the Gurvits capacity convex optimization problem, and thus our result implies an efficient deterministic algorithm for approximate counting of the lattice points up to an explicit exponential factor. We achieve our bounds by showing that the associated generating polynomials fit into a new general class of log-concave polynomials called VLC\LC (“variable-wise log-concavity”). This also implies a conjecture of Ferroni and Higashitani on the evaluations of the Ehrhart polynomials of unimodular polytopes. The essential ingredient for these results is the resolution of Barvinok’s log-concavity conjecture for contingency tables on lines, which was proven using ChatGPT 6 Astra. We conjecture a generalization of Barvinok’s conjecture, which we believe will lead to stronger and more general bounds.

1 Introduction

Totally unimodular polytopes are integral polytopes defined by a totally unimodular constraint matrix; concretely, a convex polytope QQ is totally unimodular (TU) if there exists a totally unimodular matrix MM (i.e., all minors are in {−1,0,+1}\{-1,0,+1\}) and an integral vector 𝒃\bm{b} such that Q={𝒚≥0:M​𝒚=𝒃}Q=\{\bm{y}\geq 0:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}. Such polytopes have a wide range of applications, with their lattice points often representing integer solutions to various combinatorial problems. These applications include job assignments, contingency tables, bipartite matchings, bipartite independent sets, network flows, routing configurations, and beyond.

In this paper, we address two natural questions for such polytopes:

  1. 1.

    How can we estimate the number of lattice points of such a polytope QQ?

  2. 2.

    How does the number of lattice points of QQ vary with the choice of 𝒃\bm{b}?

Answers to both of these questions arise by proving log-concavity properties of generating functions associated to totally unimodular polytopes.

Given a totally unimodular polytope Q={𝒚≥0:M​𝒚=𝒃}Q=\{\bm{y}\geq 0:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}, there is a natural generating function for its lattice points based on the choice of 𝒃\bm{b}. Concretely, if MM is m×nm\times n and has columns 𝒂1,…,𝒂n\bm{a}_{1},\ldots,\bm{a}_{n} then

PM​(𝒙)=∏j=1n11−𝒙𝒂jP_{M}(\bm{x})=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{1-\bm{x}^{\bm{a}_{j}}}

is a generating function with the property that the 𝒙𝒃\bm{x}^{\bm{b}} coefficient of PM​(𝒙)P_{M}(\bm{x}) is precisely the number of lattice points of QQ. Both of the above questions then become questions about PMP_{M}: how can we estimate the coefficients of PMP_{M}, and how can we understand how the coefficients of PMP_{M} relate to one another?

To address these questions, we prove that truncations of PMP_{M} satisfy a certain natural log-concavity property called VLC\LC. This property says that, after applying coefficient extractions and positive evaluations to all but one variable of PMP_{M}, the coefficients of the remaining polynomial are log-concave. This generalizes various notions of log-concave polynomials (strongly log-concave [30], completely log-concave [2], Lorentzian [13], etc.) which have had widespread applications in mathematics and computer science.

The fact that truncations of PMP_{M} are VLC\LC is then based on the underlying main technical result of the paper: that the coefficients of PMP_{M} are log-concave along any rational line. This says in fact that as 𝒃\bm{b} moves along any line, the number of lattice points of QQ forms a log-concave sequence. Barvinok originally asked a more general question of this form for the case of contingency tables [9], and we resolve this line version here for all TU polytopes. This gives a nice answer to question 2, while the full strength of Barvinok’s question for TU polytopes is still open Question 1.7.

The VLC\LC property then enables us also to answer question 1. The Gurvits capacity method was originally developed to give a simple proof of the van der Waerden conjecture for permanents in [29]. This technique implies a deterministic simply exponential approximation algorithm for non-negative matrix permanents as well. Since this original work, the capacity method has seen numerous applications to bounding and deterministically approximating various other combinatorial quantities. The general idea is to use log-concavity properties of a given generating function to approximate its coefficients by an associated convex optimization problem. The VLC\LC property is then tailor-made precisely to allow the Gurvits capacity method to work as usual, and thus we can apply this method to PMP_{M} and related generating functions.

1.1 Our Results

We now formally answer question 1: how can we estimate the number of lattice points of a TU polytope? We give two results in this direction. The first gives general bounds for all TU polytopes, and the second gives simply exponential bounds in a slightly restricted regime.

Theorem 1.1 (Corollary 4.5).

Let MM be an m×nm\times n totally unimodular matrix with columns 𝐚1,…,𝐚n\bm{a}_{1},\ldots,\bm{a}_{n}. For all 𝐛∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} such that #⁡{𝐲∈ℤ≥0n∣M​𝐲=𝐛}<∞\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}<\infty, we have

ℰ≥#⁡{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n∣M​𝒚=𝒃}≥e−m​(1+n​‖𝒃‖1)−m​ℰ,\mathcal{E}\geq\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}\geq e^{-m}(1+n\|\bm{b}\|_{1})^{-m}\mathcal{E},

where

ℰ=inf𝒙>0𝒙−𝒃​∏j=1n1−(𝒙𝒂j)‖𝒃‖1+11−𝒙𝒂j=inf𝒙>0𝒙−𝒃​∏j=1n∑k=0‖𝒃‖1𝒙k​𝒂j\mathcal{E}=\inf_{\bm{x}>0}\bm{x}^{-\bm{b}}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1-(\bm{x}^{\bm{a}_{j}})^{\|\bm{b}\|_{1}+1}}{1-\bm{x}^{\bm{a}_{j}}}=\inf_{\bm{x}>0}\bm{x}^{-\bm{b}}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{k=0}^{\|\bm{b}\|_{1}}\bm{x}^{k\bm{a}_{j}}

is a convex program up to log\log-log\log transformation.

Corollary 1.2 (Corollary 4.6).

Let MM be an m×nm\times n totally unimodular matrix with columns 𝐚1,…,𝐚n\bm{a}_{1},\ldots,\bm{a}_{n} and max⁡{m,n}≥3\max\{m,n\}\geq 3. For all 𝐛∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} satisfying ∥𝐛∥1≥6​m⋅log⁡(max⁡{m,n})\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}\geq 6m\cdot\log(\max\{m,n\}) and such that #⁡{𝐲∈ℤ≥0n∣M​𝐲=𝐛}<∞\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}<\infty, we have

ℰ≥#⁡{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n∣M​𝒚=𝒃}≥e−‖𝒃‖1​ℰ,\mathcal{E}\geq\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}\geq e^{-\|\bm{b}\|_{1}}\mathcal{E},

where ℰ\mathcal{E} is as in Theorem 1.1.

Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 can also be made algorithmic, using the maximum-entropy optimization framework of [41].

Theorem 1.3 (see Section 5).

There is a deterministic algorithm (based on the ellipsoid algorithm) which, given an m×nm\times n totally unimodular matrix MM, a vector 𝐛∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} such that {𝐲∈ℤ≥0n∣M​𝐲=𝐛}\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\} is nonempty, and an ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), computes 𝒜\mathcal{A} such that 𝒜−ϵ≤log⁡ℰ≤𝒜+ϵ\mathcal{A}-\epsilon\leq\log\mathcal{E}\leq\mathcal{A}+\epsilon in time polynomial in mm, nn, log⁡(1+‖𝐛‖1)\log(1+\|\bm{b}\|_{1}), and log⁡1ϵ\log\frac{1}{\epsilon}. Here ℰ\mathcal{E} is defined as in Theorem 1.1.

The proofs of Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2 are then based on our answer to question 2: how does the number of lattice points of a TU polytope vary with 𝒃\bm{b}? The following result answers this by generalizing a question of Barvinok [9] on the log-concavity of the counts of contingency tables with various marginals. Our result in fact holds for unimodular polytopes, which are defined like totally unimodular polytopes except that the defining matrix MM is only required to be unimodular.

Theorem 1.4 (Theorem 3.1).

Let MM be an m×nm\times n (not necessarily totally) unimodular matrix. For all 𝐛,𝐛−,𝐛+∈ℤm\bm{b},\bm{b}^{-},\bm{b}^{+}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} such that 𝐛=𝐛−+𝐛+2\bm{b}=\frac{\bm{b}^{-}+\bm{b}^{+}}{2}, we have

#​{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n∣M​𝒚=𝒃}2≥#⁡{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n∣M​𝒚=𝒃−}⋅#⁡{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n∣M​𝒚=𝒃+},\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}^{2}\geq\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid M\bm{y}=\bm{b}^{-}\}\cdot\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid M\bm{y}=\bm{b}^{+}\},

given that all of these fibers are finite.

We note that Theorem 1.4 immediately implies a recent conjecture for TU polytopes on the log-concavity of Ehrhart evaluations. This conjecture comes from [21], where the authors in fact make the conjecture for all IDP lattice polytopes (though this is now false in general by [22]). Recall that, given a lattice polytope PP, the Ehrhart polynomial EP​(t)E_{P}(t) is the unique polynomial such that EP​(k)=#⁡(k​P∩ℤn)E_{P}(k)=\#\left(kP\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}\right) for all k∈ℤ≥0k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}.

Corollary 1.5 (Conjecture 1.2 of [21]).

For all (not necessarily totally) unimodular polytopes PP, we have EP​(k)2≥EP​(k−1)⋅EP​(k+1)E_{P}(k)^{2}\geq E_{P}(k-1)\cdot E_{P}(k+1) for all k∈ℤ≥1k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}.

Beyond our main results, we can also prove slightly stronger results under further restrictions. We give various bounds in Section 4, and we give one such result here to demonstrate the sort of thing we can achieve.

Let MM be an m×nm\times n totally unimodular matrix with columns 𝐚1,…,𝐚n\bm{a}_{1},\ldots,\bm{a}_{n} such that 𝐚i≠𝟎\bm{a}_{i}\neq\bm{0} for all i∈[n]i\in[n], and let 𝐬i\bm{s}_{i} be the sum of the first ii rows of MM for i∈[m]i\in[m]. 1.2 An Open Question

Theorem 1.4 is in fact based upon a stronger coefficient-wise positivity result (Theorem 3.1) which follows from the bijective proof which we give in Section 3. This theorem raises an open question, which is the natural generalization of Barvinok’s question in [9].

Question 1.7.

Let M∈ℤm×nM\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n} be a unimodular matrix and μ\mu a probability distribution on ℤm\mathbb{Z}^{m} (perhaps with finite support) such that its mean is 𝐛∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}. Is it that case that

#⁡{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n∣M​𝒚=𝒃}≥∏𝒂∈ℤm#​{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n∣M​𝒚=𝒂}μ⁡(𝒂)​?\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}\geq\prod_{\bm{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}}\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}\mid M\bm{y}=\bm{a}\}^{\mu(\bm{a})}?

Note that for functions/distributions over ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, Question 1.7 would immediately follow from Theorem 1.4. However, for functions/distributions over ℤm\mathbb{Z}^{m}, convexity on lines does not imply global convexity in general.

We believe that a positive answer to Question 1.7 would enable us to obtain stronger capacity bounds (hopefully simply exponential) in general, using the following idea. Currently, most capacity bounds are proved inductively on each variable of a given polynomial or generating series. Because of this, the bounds often depend on distances of the desired marginals or degree vector (e.g. the 𝒃\bm{b} vector) to the boundary of the Newton polyhedron in the coordinate directions. The coordinate direction distance can be very bad for general TU polytopes, and so we need to adapt the application of the capacity bounds to handle this. Given the inequalities of Question 1.7, it is perhaps possible that this capacity induction argument may be able to be exchanged with a geometric argument related to distances to the boundary of the Newton polyhedron in any choice of directions. This would yield much better bounds and approximation factors, if possible.

1.3 Previous and Related Work

Bounding and approximately counting lattice points in totally unimodular polytopes has attracted considerable attention. A variety of bounds and approximation algorithms, both randomized and deterministic, are known for important classes of such polytopes. On the randomized side, fully polynomial randomized approximation schemes (FPRASs) have been obtained for bipartite perfect matchings [33], binary contingency tables [12], and nonnegative integer contingency tables under restrictions such as a fixed number of rows or sufficiently large margins [16, 20, 39]. Related results apply to cell-bounded contingency tables with a fixed number of rows and to integral flows with sufficiently large tight capacities [15]. For certain classes of smooth margins, a randomized approximation algorithm runs in time quasipolynomial in the total sum of the table entries [8]. More recently, rapid mixing of the natural swap chain was established for binary contingency tables with arbitrary feasible margins [23].

On the deterministic side, matrix scaling and polynomial capacity methods give polynomial-time exponential approximations for counting bipartite perfect matchings [37, 28, 29], with subsequent improvements [27, 4]. Recent preprints obtain a subexponential approximation factor [34] and a (1+ε)n(1+\varepsilon)^{n} approximation factor for every fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0 [19], where nn is the number of vertices on each side of the bipartition. Convex optimization and polynomial capacity methods also give (often simply) exponential estimates for contingency tables [10, 11, 31, 14] and integer flows [10, 36, 35]. Computationally efficient asymptotic formulas are available in suitable smooth-margin regimes [6]. For contingency tables with a fixed number of rows, deterministic fully polynomial-time approximation schemes (FPTASs) are known [24], with improved running times in the two-row case [1].

Beyond these special classes, other positive results include polynomial-time exact counting in fixed dimension [7], exact counting methods for nonnegative totally unimodular systems with a fixed number of equations [40], algebraic methods for computing counting polynomials for unimodular systems [18], and maximum-entropy Gaussian approximations under well-roundedness assumptions [5].

In contrast, no fully polynomial randomized or deterministic approximation scheme is known for arbitrary totally unimodular polytopes; such an algorithm would in particular yield an FPRAS for counting independent sets in bipartite graphs [26]. This motivates seeking weaker approximation guarantees that apply uniformly to all bounded TU polytopes, which is what we prove here.

1.4 AI Declaration

The AI tool we specifically used was ChatGPT 6 Astra. The authors have verified and take full responsibility for everything written in the paper.

Before the first draft.

The resolution of Barvinok’s conjecture/question on the log-concavity on lines of the contingency tables counts (Theorem 1.4) was the main AI input to this paper. We generalized this result to all TU polytopes with upper and lower entrywise bounds on the counted lattice points (Theorem 3.1), and in fact the AI suggested in a remark that this should be possible. Beyond that, the literature review and much of the associated parts of the introduction were written with the help of AI.

After the first draft.

We used AI to check for errors or to make suggestions on the flow or style of the paper. From this we fixed a number of errors which were mostly minor; the main issue that was fixed here were proofs regarding limiting arguments for capacity and for sequences of Laurent polynomials and series. In particular Lemma 4.11 and the surrounding results were added at this point. Additionally, AI also suggested a way to improve the bound in Theorem 1.1 via Lemma 4.3. We also originally had referenced [41, 42] as the way to prove algorithmic efficiency in Theorem 1.3, but we had left out the details. We used AI to fill in those details, and now we have the proof of Theorem 1.3 in Section 5. Further, AI also found that the central-fiber argument in our (AI-assisted) proof of Theorem 1.4 has a direct antecedent in the graph-orientation argument of [17]. Finally, AI also suggested many changes to the structure, ordering, and content of the introduction and title. We took many of those suggestions, and then wrote the new introduction ourselves.

2 VLC\LC Laurent polynomials

Gurvits’ capacity function has been widely used to obtain lower bounds for various interesting combinatorial quantities. The underlying idea of these results is that if a (Laurent) polynomial has a certain log-concavity property, then one could use the theory of log-concave polynomials to derive lower bounds for its coefficients. However, currently studied log-concavity properties (e.g., Lorentzian, denormalized/dually Lorentzian, etc.) are all conditions which are too strong to apply to TU polytopes in general.

Thus, in Section 2.1 we introduce a class of Laurent polynomials with weaker log-concavity properties, for which capacity lower bounds are still applicable. We further explore basic properties of this class throughout Section 2.2. We then turn our focus to unimodular and totally unimodular (TU) matrices in Section 3 and prove that the cardinalities of the fibers of a unimodular polytope are log-concave along lines.

2.1 Definition and capacity bounds

There are two key steps in proving capacity bounds for a denormalized Lorentzian polynomial pp: first that any evaluation of pp in all but one variable is a univariate polynomial with log-concave coefficients, and second that [xiαi]​p[x_{i}^{\alpha_{i}}]p satisfies the first condition for any i,αii,\alpha_{i}. We will take these two properties and define a new class of Laurent polynomials. Capacity lower bounds then naturally extend to this class.

Recall that a sequence {ak}k∈ℤ\{a_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} of non-negative numbers is said to be log-concave if it has no internal zeros and ak2≥ak−1⋅ak+1a_{k}^{2}\geq a_{k-1}\cdot a_{k+1} for any valid index kk. A Laurent polynomial is a sum p⁡(𝒙)=∑𝜶∈ℤnp𝜶​𝒙𝜶p(\bm{x})=\sum_{\bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}p_{\bm{\alpha}}\bm{x^{\alpha}} with a finite support, where the support of pp denoted by supp⁡(p)\supp(p) is the set {𝜶∈ℤn:p𝜶≠0}\{\bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}:p_{\bm{\alpha}}\neq 0\}. We further say that a univariate Laurent polynomial p⁡(x)=∑k∈ℤpk​xkp(x)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}p_{k}x^{k} has a log-concave coefficient sequence if {pk}k∈ℤ\{p_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} is a log-concave sequence.

Definition 2.1.

Define:

VLC1={p⁡(x)∈ℝ⁡[x±1]:p​ has a log-concave coefficient sequence}.\LC_{1}=\{p(x)\in\mathbb{R}[x^{\pm 1}]:p\text{ has a log-concave coefficient sequence}\}.

and for any n≥2n\geq 2, let VLCn\LC_{n} contain all nn-variate Laurent polynomials p⁡(x1,⋯,xn)=∑𝜶∈ℤnp𝜶​𝒙𝜶p(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})=\sum_{\bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}p_{\bm{\alpha}}\bm{x^{\alpha}} with non-negative coefficients such that:

  • •

    Evaluating pp at any n−1n-1 variables with positive real numbers belongs to VLC1\LC_{1},

  • •

    [xiαi]​p[x_{i}^{\alpha_{i}}]p is in VLCn−1\LC_{n-1} for any i∈[n]i\in[n] and αi∈ℤ\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}.

Equivalently, p⁡(x1,⋯,xn)∈ℝ≥0​[𝒙,𝒙−1]p(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}[\bm{x},\bm{x}^{-1}] is an element of VLCn\LC_{n} if for any S⊆[n]S\subseteq[n] and any 𝜶∈ℤS\bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{Z}^{S}, any positive evaluation of [∏i∈Sxiαi]​p[\prod_{i\in S}{x}_{i}^{{\alpha}_{i}}]p in all but one variable has log-concave coefficients. In a sense, the coefficients of pp are log-concave after applying certain variable-wise operations, hence the name VLC\LC.

More generally, we will say that a polynomial p⁡(x1,⋯,xn)p(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}) is VLC\LC if it belongs to VLCn\LC_{n}.

Lorentzian polynomials and denormalized Lorentzian polynomials are both subclasses of VLC\LC (see [13, §3.1]). In fact, this class of Laurent polynomials is crafted in a way that the capacity bound for the coefficients of denormalized Lorentzian Polynomials extends naturally to VLC\LC Laurent polynomials.

2.2 Examples and properties

As mentioned before, any denormalized Lorentzian polynomial is VLC\LC. It is easy to see that any “shift” of a denormalized Lorentzian polynomial is also VLC\LC, i.e. 𝒙𝜶​p​(𝒙)\bm{x^{\alpha}}p(\bm{x}) is VLC\LC if pp is denormalized Lorentzian. However, the class of VLC\LC Laurent polynomials contains a much larger set of Laurent polynomials. The following is an example of a Laurent polynomial that is not necessarily denormalized Lorentzian but is VLC\LC:

Example 2.3.

Let n,k∈ℤ≥0n,k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} and 𝒃∈{0,±1}n\bm{b}\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{n}, then:

p⁡(x1,⋯,xn)=∑t=0k𝒙t⋅𝒃p(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})=\sum_{t=0}^{k}\bm{x}^{t\cdot\bm{b}}

is VLC\LC. We proceed by induction on nn. If n=1n=1, the statement is trivial since the coefficients sequence of pp is the all ones sequence. Now suppose n≥2n\geq 2 and assume the statement holds for n−1n-1. Let us check both of the conditions of Definition 2.1 for pp.

First evaluate pp at all but one variable, say xix_{i}. It is easy to check that the coefficients of the polynomial p⁡(𝒙)|xj=rj​∀j≠i{\left.\kern-1.2ptp(\bm{x})\vphantom{\big|}\right|_{x_{j}=r_{j}\forall j\neq i}} form a geometric sequence and thus are log-concave. Furthermore, if bi≠0b_{i}\neq 0, the Laurent polynomial [xiαi]​p​(𝒙)[x_{i}^{\alpha_{i}}]p(\bm{x}) is either the zero polynomial or just a monomial and is VLC\LC. If bi=0b_{i}=0 however, [xiαi]​p[x_{i}^{\alpha_{i}}]p is really a Laurent polynomial in n−1n-1 variables which is VLC\LC by the induction hypothesis.

As another example, suppose 𝒃1,𝒃2∈{0,1}n\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, then the series:

q⁡(𝒙)=∑t=0k𝒙t⋅𝒃1⋅∑t=0k𝒙t⋅𝒃2q(\bm{x})=\sum_{t=0}^{k}\bm{x}^{t\cdot\bm{b}_{1}}\cdot\sum_{t=0}^{k}\bm{x}^{t\cdot\bm{b}_{2}}

can also be shown to be VLC\LC by basic algebra and some extra effort. We have refrained from including the details of this proof for brevity. One could see that this polynomial is indeed VLC\LC by Proposition 3.8.

For general 𝒃,𝒃1,𝒃2\bm{b},\bm{b}_{1},\bm{b}_{2}, the supports of the Laurent polynomials pp and qq in Example 2.3 need not be MM-convex. Thus, neither is necessarily a denormalized Lorentzian Laurent polynomial. This raises the question of characterizing the support of an VLC\LC Laurent polynomial.

Proposition 2.4.

If p⁡(𝐱)=∑𝛂∈ℤnp𝛂​𝐱𝛂p(\bm{x})=\sum_{\bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}p_{\bm{\alpha}}\bm{x^{\alpha}} is an VLC\LC Laurent polynomial, then its support is a finite saturated set.

S⊆ℤnS\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{n} is called a saturated set if S=conv⁡(S)∩ℤnS=\conv(S)\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}, where conv⁡(S)\conv(S) is the convex hull of SS.

Before proving this proposition, let us recall a well-known fact about newt⁡(p):=conv⁡(supp⁡(p))\newt(p):=\conv(\supp(p)), also known as the Newton polytope of pp.

Fact 2.5 ([3, Fact 2.18], see also [35, Lemma 4.15]).

If pp is a nonzero Laurent polynomial (or a Laurent series with a nonempty domain of convergence and a closed Newton polyhedron) with nonnegative coefficients, then cap𝜶⁡(p)>0\cpc_{\bm{\alpha}}(p)>0 iff α∈newt⁡(p)\alpha\in\newt(p).

Proof of Proposition 2.4.

It suffices to show that p𝜶>0p_{\bm{\alpha}}>0 for any 𝜶∈newt⁡(p)∩ℤn\bm{\alpha}\in\newt(p)\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}. By Fact 2.5, for any such 𝜶\bm{\alpha}, cap𝜶⁡(p)>0\cpc_{\bm{\alpha}}(p)>0. Thus, by Proposition 2.2, we have:

p𝜶≥cap𝜶⁡(p)⋅∏i=1n|βi−αi||βi−αi|(1+|βi−αi|)1+|βi−αi|>0.p_{\bm{\alpha}}\geq\cpc_{\bm{\alpha}}(p)\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{|\beta_{i}-\alpha_{i}|^{|\beta_{i}-\alpha_{i}|}}{(1+|\beta_{i}-\alpha_{i}|)^{1+|\beta_{i}-\alpha_{i}|}}>0.

∎

One would hope that any finite saturated set would be the support of some VLC\LC Laurent polynomial, but this is not the case. For instance, the set S={(0,0),(1,0),(2,1)}S=\{(0,0),(1,0),(2,1)\} is a saturated set, but the polynomial p⁡(x,y)=a+b​x+c​x2​yp(x,y)=a+bx+cx^{2}y is not VLC\LC no matter the choice of a,b,c>0a,b,c>0. This is because evaluating yy at a large enough r>0r>0 breaks log-concavity of the sequence a,b,c​ra,b,cr. We currently do not have a necessary and sufficient condition for a set SS to arise the support of an VLC\LC Laurent polynomial.

Proposition 2.6.

The class of VLC\LC Laurent polynomials is closed under scaling variables.

Proof.

We proceed by induction on the number of variables. If p⁡(x)=∑k∈ℤpk​xkp(x)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}p_{k}x^{k} has a log-concave coefficient sequence, then so does p⁡(c​x)=∑k∈ℤck​pk​xkp(cx)=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}c^{k}p_{k}x^{k}, and the induction basis holds.

Let n≥2n\geq 2 and let p⁡(x1,⋯,xn)p(x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}) be an VLC\LC Laurent polynomial and let c>0c>0. We want to show that q⁡(𝒙)=p⁡(c​x1,x2,⋯,xn)q(\bm{x})=p(cx_{1},x_{2},\cdots,x_{n}) is also an VLC\LC Laurent polynomial. Any evaluation of qq at all but the variable xix_{i} where i≠1i\neq 1 has log-concave coefficients, since:

q(𝒙)|xj=rj,j≠i=p(𝒙)|x1=cr1,xj=rjj≠i,1.{\left.\kern-1.2ptq(\bm{x})\vphantom{\big|}\right|_{x_{j}=r_{j},j\neq i}}={\left.\kern-1.2ptp(\bm{x})\vphantom{\big|}\right|_{x_{1}=cr_{1},x_{j}=r_{j}j\neq i,1}}.

If qq is evaluated at all but variables except x1x_{1}, then:

q⁡(x1,r2,⋯,rn)=p⁡(c​x1,r2,⋯,xn)=∑k∈ℤpk​ck​x1k,q(x_{1},r_{2},\cdots,r_{n})=p(cx_{1},r_{2},\cdots,x_{n})=\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}p_{k}c^{k}x_{1}^{k},

where pkp_{k} is the coefficient of x1kx_{1}^{k} in p⁡(x1,r2,⋯,rn)p(x_{1},r_{2},\cdots,r_{n}). Since pp is VLC\LC, the sequence {pk}k∈ℤ\{p_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} is log-concave, and therefore, so is the sequence {ck​pk}k∈ℤ\{c^{k}p_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}. Hence any evaluation of qq in n−1n-1 variables has log-concave coefficients.

Furthermore, we know that [xiα]​p[x_{i}^{\alpha}]p is an VLC\LC Laurent polynomial in n−1n-1 variables for any α∈ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{Z} and i∈[n]i\in[n]. By the induction hypothesis, for any i≠1i\neq 1, the Laurent polynomial [xiα]​q=([xiα]​p)​(c​x1,⋯,xi−1,xi+1,⋯,xn)[x_{i}^{\alpha}]q=([x_{i}^{\alpha}]p)(cx_{1},\cdots,x_{i-1},x_{i+1},\cdots,x_{n}) is VLC\LC as well. Lastly, [x1α]​q=cα​[x1α]​p[x_{1}^{\alpha}]q=c^{\alpha}[x_{1}^{\alpha}]p is VLC\LC too and and we are done. ∎

Proposition 2.7.

If a sequence {pi​(𝐱)}i≥0\{p_{i}(\bm{x})\}_{i\geq 0} of VLCn\LC_{n} Laurent polynomials converges coefficient-wise to a Laurent polynomial p⁡(𝐱)p(\bm{x}) such that supp⁡(pi)⊆supp⁡(p)\supp(p_{i})\subseteq\supp(p) for all i≥0i\geq 0, then p∈VLCnp\in\LC_{n}.

Proof.

Proceed with induction on nn. The statement for n=1n=1 follows from the fact that the limit of any log-concave sequence is a log-concave sequence. Let n≥2n\geq 2. Suppose r2,⋯,rn>0r_{2},\cdots,r_{n}>0. Then:

p⁡(x1,r2,⋯,rn)=limi→∞pi​(x1,r2,⋯,rn),p(x_{1},r_{2},\cdots,r_{n})=\lim_{i\to\infty}p_{i}(x_{1},r_{2},\cdots,r_{n}),

since each pi​(x1,r2,⋯,rn)p_{i}(x_{1},r_{2},\cdots,r_{n}) has a log-concave coefficient sequence, the coefficient sequence of p⁡(x1,r2,⋯,rn)p(x_{1},r_{2},\cdots,r_{n}) is log-concave as well. Moreover, for any α∈ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}, j∈[n]j\in[n]:

[xjα]​p=limi→∞[xjα]​pi.[x_{j}^{\alpha}]p=\lim_{i\to\infty}[x_{j}^{\alpha}]p_{i}.

Since supp⁡([xjα]​pi)⊆supp⁡([xjα]​p)\supp([x_{j}^{\alpha}]p_{i})\subseteq\supp([x_{j}^{\alpha}]p) for all i≥0i\geq 0, [xjα]​p[x_{j}^{\alpha}]p is VLCn−1\LC_{n-1} by the induction hypothesis, finishing the proof. ∎

3 Unimodular and Totally unimodular (TU) polytopes

The goal of this section is to prove the following log-concavity statement:

(∑M​𝒚=𝒃++𝒃−2𝒌1≤𝒚≤𝒌2𝒘𝒚)2≥∑M​𝒚=𝒃+𝒌1≤𝒚≤𝒌2𝒘𝒚⋅∑M​𝒚=𝒃−𝒌1≤𝒚≤𝒌2𝒘𝒚,\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\bm{y}=\frac{\bm{b}^{+}+\bm{b}^{-}}{2}\\ \bm{k}_{1}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}_{2}\end{subarray}}\bm{w^{y}}\right)^{2}\geq\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\bm{y}={\bm{b}^{+}}\\ \bm{k}_{1}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}_{2}\end{subarray}}\bm{w^{y}}\cdot\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}M\bm{y}={\bm{b}^{-}}\\ \bm{k}_{1}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}_{2}\end{subarray}}\bm{w^{y}},

where MM is an m×nm\times n unimodular matrix and 𝒃+,𝒃−,𝒃++𝒃−2∈ℤm,𝒘∈ℝ>0n\bm{b}^{+},\bm{b}^{-},\frac{\bm{b}^{+}+\bm{b}^{-}}{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m},\bm{w}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} are given vectors. Recall that a matrix MM is said to be unimodular if all of its non-singular rank⁡(M)×rank⁡(M)\rank(M)\times\rank(M) submatrices have determinant ±1\pm 1. We will provide an AI-assisted proof that this sequence is log-concave for any MM and 𝒃\bm{b} in Section 3.1. In Section 3.2, we will use this log-concavity statement to show that ∑𝟎≤𝒚≤𝒌𝒙M​𝒚\sum_{\bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}}\bm{x}^{M\bm{y}} is an VLC\LC Laurent polynomial for any TU matrix MM. We will then derive capacity bounds for #{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n:M𝒚=𝒃,𝒚≤𝒌}\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b},\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}\} using this Laurent polynomial in Section 4.

3.1 Mid point log-concavity for unimodular polytopes

The ideas and proofs in this section follow an AI assisted argument for midpoint log-concavity of contingency tables with tweaks to prove what we require for our purposes. In particular, the proofs of Theorem 3.1, Lemma 3.2 and Lemma 3.3 are AI-assisted. We note that the pair-decomposition and induction used in Lemma 3.2 and Lemma 3.3 generalize the argument from Section 5 of [17] from graph orientations to lattice points in boxes subject to unimodular linear constraints.

For any unimodular matrix M∈ℤm×nM\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n} and any vectors 𝒃,𝒂,𝒌1,𝒌2\bm{b},\bm{a},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2} of proper dimensions, Define:

ℬ(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(M,𝒃)\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(M,\bm{b}) ={𝒚:M𝒚=𝒃,𝒌1≤𝒚≤𝒌2},\displaystyle=\{\bm{y}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b},\bm{k}_{1}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}_{2}\},
B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(M,𝒃)\displaystyle B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(M,\bm{b}) =|ℬ(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(𝒃)∩ℤn|,\displaystyle=|\mathcal{B}_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b})\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}|,
ℰ⁡(M,𝒂)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}(M,\bm{a}) ={𝒚:M𝒚=M​𝒂2,yi∈{0,ai}∀i∈[n]},\displaystyle=\{\bm{y}:M\bm{y}=\frac{M\bm{a}}{2},y_{i}\in\{0,a_{i}\}\forall i\in[n]\},
E⁡(M,𝒂)\displaystyle E(M,\bm{a}) =|ℰ⁡(M,𝒂)|,\displaystyle=|\mathcal{E}(M,\bm{a})|,
T⁡(M,𝒃,𝒌1,𝒌2,𝒘)\displaystyle T(M,\bm{b},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2};\bm{w}) =∑𝒌1≤𝒚≤𝒌2M​𝒚=𝒃𝒘𝒚.\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{k}_{1}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}_{2}\\ M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\end{subarray}}\bm{w}^{\bm{y}}.

When the choice of the matrix MM is clear from context, we will omit MM from the notation in all of the definitions above. Note that if E⁡(M,𝒂)≠0E(M,\bm{a})\neq 0, then we must have M​𝒂∈(2​ℤ)m{M\bm{a}}\in(2\mathbb{Z})^{m}. We aim to prove the following theorem:

Theorem 3.1.

Suppose 𝐛,𝐛+,𝐛−\bm{b,b^{+},b^{-}} are integer vectors such that 𝐛=𝐛++𝐛−2\bm{b}=\frac{\bm{b^{+}}+\bm{b^{-}}}{2}. Then for any 𝐤1,𝐤2\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}:

T​(𝒃,𝒌1,𝒌2,𝒘)2−T⁡(𝒃+,𝒌1,𝒌2,𝒘)⋅T⁡(𝒃−,𝒌1,𝒌2,𝒘)T(\bm{b},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2};\bm{w})^{2}-T(\bm{b^{+}},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2};\bm{w})\cdot T(\bm{b^{-}},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2};\bm{w})

is a Laurent polynomial in 𝐰\bm{w} with nonnegative coefficients.

In fact, we will explicitly express the coefficients of T​(𝒃,𝒌1,𝒌2,𝒘)2−T⁡(𝒃+,𝒌1,𝒌2,𝒘)⋅T⁡(𝒃−,𝒌1,𝒌2,𝒘)T(\bm{b},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2};\bm{w})^{2}-T(\bm{b^{+}},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2};\bm{w})\cdot T(\bm{b^{-}},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2};\bm{w}) in terms of B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(𝒃)B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b}), B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(𝒃+)B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b}^{+}) and B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(𝒃−)B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b}^{-}) and prove that these coefficients are non-negative using Lemma 3.2, Lemma 3.3 and Lemma 3.4. We then use Theorem 3.1 to prove that the Ehrhart of a unimodular polytope has log-concave evaluations, see Corollary 3.5. We explain why our methods do not work for a general IDP polytope in Remark 3.6.

Lemma 3.2.

For any integer vector 𝐛∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}, we have:

B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(𝒃)2=∑𝒂∈ℤn𝟎≤𝒂≤𝒌2−𝒌1,E⁡(𝒂)>0E⁡(𝒂)​B(𝒌1,𝒌2−𝒂)​(𝒃−M​𝒂2).B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b})^{2}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\ \bm{0}\leq\bm{a}\leq\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{k}_{1},\\ E(\bm{a})>0\end{subarray}}E(\bm{a})B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{a})}\left(\bm{b}-\frac{M\bm{a}}{2}\right).

where for any number r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}, we define (r)+=0(r)_{+}=0 if r<0r<0 and (r)+=r(r)_{+}=r otherwise. The following facts are easy to check:

  1. 1.

    𝒙=𝒎+𝒑\bm{x}=\bm{m}+\bm{p},

  2. 2.

    𝒚=𝒎+𝒂−𝒑\bm{y}=\bm{m}+\bm{a}-\bm{p},

  3. 3.

    2​𝒑=𝒂+𝒙−𝒚2\bm{p}=\bm{a}+\bm{x}-\bm{y} so M​𝒑=M​𝒂2M\bm{p}=\frac{M\bm{a}}{2} and further pi∈{0,ai}p_{i}\in\{0,a_{i}\}, thus 𝒑∈ℰ⁡(𝒂)\bm{p}\in\mathcal{E}(\bm{a}),

  4. 4.

    2​𝒎=𝒙+𝒚−𝒂2\bm{m}=\bm{x}+\bm{y}-\bm{a}, so M​𝒎=𝒃−M​𝒂2M\bm{m}=\bm{b}-\frac{M\bm{a}}{2}. Moreover 𝒌1≤𝒎≤𝒌2−𝒂\bm{k}_{1}\leq\bm{m}\leq\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{a}. Thus 𝒎∈ℬ(𝒌1,𝒌2−𝒂)​(𝒃−M​𝒂2)∩ℤn\bm{m}\in\mathcal{B}_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{a})}\left(\bm{b}-\frac{M\bm{a}}{2}\right)\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}.

Let: φ⁡(𝒙,𝒚)=(𝒂,𝒑,𝒎).\varphi(\bm{x},\bm{y})=(\bm{a},\bm{p},\bm{m}). Then φ\varphi is a bijection between the desired sets by 1 through 4. ∎

Lemma 3.3.

Given integer vectors 𝐤1≤𝐤2\bm{k}_{1}\leq\bm{k}_{2} and 𝐛\bm{b} with proper dimensions, define 𝐤:=𝐤2+𝐤1\bm{k}:=\bm{k}_{2}+\bm{k}_{1}. If M​𝐤M\bm{k} is even, then we have:

B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(𝒃)≤B(𝒌𝟏,𝒌𝟐)​(M​𝒌2).B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b})\leq B_{\bm{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}}\left(\frac{M\bm{k}}{2}\right).

Thus the base case holds.

By Lemma 3.2, write:

B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(𝒃)2=∑𝒂∈ℤn𝟎≤𝒂≤𝒌2−𝒌1E⁡(𝒂)>0E⁡(𝒂)​B(𝒌1,𝒌2−𝒂)​(𝒃−M​𝒂2),B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b})^{2}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\ \bm{0}\leq\bm{a}\leq\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{k}_{1}\\ E(\bm{a})>0\end{subarray}}E(\bm{a})B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{a})}\left(\bm{b}-\frac{M\bm{a}}{2}\right),

and:

B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(M​𝒌2)2=∑𝒂∈ℤn𝟎≤𝒂≤𝒌2−𝒌1E⁡(𝒂)>0E⁡(𝒂)​B(𝒌1,𝒌2−𝒂)​(M⁡(𝒌−𝒂)2).B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}\left(\frac{M\bm{k}}{2}\right)^{2}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\\ \bm{0}\leq\bm{a}\leq\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{k}_{1}\\ E(\bm{a})>0\end{subarray}}E(\bm{a})B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{a})}\left(\frac{M(\bm{k-a})}{2}\right).

The term 𝒂=𝟎\bm{a}=\bm{0} contributes B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(𝒃)B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b}) and B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(M​𝒌2)B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}\left(\frac{M\bm{k}}{2}\right) to the right hand sides of the first and the second identity respectively. By moving these terms to the left hand side, we get:

B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(𝒃)2−B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(𝒃)=∑𝒂∈ℤn,𝒂≠𝟎𝟎≤𝒂≤𝒌2−𝒌1E⁡(𝒂)>0E⁡(𝒂)​B(𝒌1,𝒌2−𝒂)​(𝒃−M​𝒂2),B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b})^{2}-B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n},\,\bm{a}\neq\bm{0}\\ \bm{0}\leq\bm{a}\leq\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{k}_{1}\\ E(\bm{a})>0\end{subarray}}E(\bm{a})B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{a})}\left(\bm{b}-\frac{M\bm{a}}{2}\right),

and:

B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(M​𝒌2)2−B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(M​𝒌2)=∑𝒂∈ℤn,𝒂≠𝟎𝟎≤𝒂≤𝒌2−𝒌1E⁡(𝒂)>0E⁡(𝒂)​B(𝒌1,𝒌2−𝒂)​(M⁡(𝒌−𝒂)2).B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}\left(\frac{M\bm{k}}{2}\right)^{2}-B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}\left(\frac{M\bm{k}}{2}\right)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{a}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n},\,\bm{a}\neq\bm{0}\\ \bm{0}\leq\bm{a}\leq\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{k}_{1}\\ E(\bm{a})>0\end{subarray}}E(\bm{a})B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{a})}\left(\frac{M(\bm{k-a})}{2}\right).

By induction hypothesis, for any 𝟎≤𝒂≤𝒌2−𝒌1,𝒂≠𝟎\bm{0}\leq\bm{a}\leq\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{k}_{1},\bm{a}\neq\bm{0}:

B(𝒌1,𝒌2−𝒂)​(𝒃−M​𝒂2)≤B(𝒌1,𝒌2−𝒂)​(M⁡(𝒌−𝒂)2),B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{a})}\left(\bm{b}-\frac{M\bm{a}}{2}\right)\leq B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}-\bm{a})}\left(\frac{M(\bm{k}-\bm{a})}{2}\right),

Thus B(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(M​𝒌2)≥1B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\frac{M\bm{k}}{2})\geq 1 for any 𝒌\bm{k}, fixing the issue. ∎

Lemma 3.4.

Suppose M∈ℤm×nM\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n} is a unimodular matrix and 𝐛∈ℤm,𝐤1,𝐤2∈ℤn\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}. If the polytope ℬ(𝐤1,𝐤2)(𝐛)={𝐲:M𝐲=𝐛,𝐤1≤𝐲≤𝐤2}\mathcal{B}_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b})=\{\bm{y}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b},\bm{k}_{1}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}_{2}\} is nonempty, then all of its vertices are integral.

Proof.

Let r=rank⁡(M)r=\rank(M) and fix 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*} to be a vertex of ℬ(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(M,𝒃)\mathcal{B}_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(M,\bm{b}). We say that a constraint k1,i≤yik_{1,i}\leq y_{i} or yi≤k2,iy_{i}\leq k_{2,i} is active at 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*} if it holds with equality for 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*}. The equality constraints M​𝒚∗=𝒃M\bm{y}^{*}=\bm{b} are automatically active.

Without loss of generality, assume that the first rr rows of MM are linearly independent, and let M[r]M_{[r]} be the submatrix of MM containing these rr rows, and let 𝒃[r]\bm{b}_{[r]} be the vector 𝒃\bm{b} restricted to its first rr entries.

Note that the normal vectors of the active constraints of ℬ𝒌1,𝒌2​(𝒃)\mathcal{B}_{\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}}(\bm{b}) at 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*} must span ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Otherwise there will exist some 𝒗∈ℝn\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} orthogonal to all of the active constraints. Therefore, any point 𝒚∗±ϵ​𝒗\bm{y}^{*}\pm\epsilon\bm{v} belongs to PP for small enough ϵ∈ℝ≥0\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, contradicting the assumption that 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*} is a vertex of MM.

So in addition to the rr constraints of M[r]M_{[r]} that are automatically active at 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*}, there are (at least) n−rn-r constraints of 𝒌1≤𝒚≤𝒌2\bm{k}_{1}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}_{2} that are active at 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*} and are linearly independent together with the equality constraints of M[r]M_{[r]}. After permuting the columns of MM, assume that yi=diy_{i}=d_{i} for i∈[n−r]i\in[n-r] where di∈{k1,i,k2,i}d_{i}\in\{k_{1,i},k_{2,i}\}. For simplicity, let AA be the submatrix of the first n−rn-r columns of M[r]M_{[r]} and BB its last rr columns, so that M[r]=[AB]M_{[r]}=\begin{bmatrix}A&B\end{bmatrix}. We know that 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*} satisfies:

[ABid(n−r)×(n−r)0(n−r)×r]​𝒚∗=[𝒃[r]𝒅],det[ABid(n−r)×(n−r)0(n−r)×r]≠0,\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\ \mathrm{id}_{(n-r)\times(n-r)}&0_{(n-r)\times r}\end{bmatrix}\bm{y}^{*}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{b}_{[r]}\\ \bm{d}\end{bmatrix},\det\begin{bmatrix}A&B\\ \mathrm{id}_{(n-r)\times(n-r)}&0_{(n-r)\times r}\end{bmatrix}\neq 0,

In particular, we must have detB≠0\det{B}\neq 0. Since BB is a non-singular r×rr\times r submatrix of MM, its determinant is either +1+1 or −1-1 and B−1B^{-1} is an integer matrix. Thus:

yj∗=[B−1​(𝒃[r]−A​𝒅)]j∈ℤ,∀j∈{n−r+1,⋯,n}{y}^{*}_{j}=\left[B^{-1}(\bm{b}_{[r]}-A\bm{d})\right]_{j}\in\mathbb{Z},\quad\forall j\in\{n-r+1,\cdots,n\}

and 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*} is an integer point. ∎

We now have all the tools to prove Theorem 3.1.

Corollary 3.5.

Let M∈ℤm×nM\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n} be a unimodular matrix and 𝐛∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}. Suppose P={𝐲∈ℝ≥0n:M​𝐲=𝐛}P=\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\} is a bounded polytope. Then EP​(t)2≥EP​(t−1)⋅EP​(t+1)E_{P}(t)^{2}\geq E_{P}(t-1)\cdot E_{P}(t+1) for all t∈ℤ≥1t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}.

Proof.

By Theorem 3.1:

T​(t​𝒃,𝟎,𝒌,𝟏)2≥T⁡((t−1)​𝒃,𝟎,𝒌,𝟏)⋅T⁡((t+1)​𝒃,𝟎,𝒌,𝟏)T(t\bm{b},\bm{0},\bm{k};\bm{1})^{2}\geq T((t-1)\bm{b},\bm{0},\bm{k};\bm{1})\cdot T\left((t+1)\bm{b},\bm{0},\bm{k};\bm{1}\right)

As 𝒌\bm{k} tends to ∞\infty coordinate-wise we get:

#​{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝒚=t​𝒃}2≥#⁡{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝒚=(t−1)​𝒃}⋅#⁡{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝒚=(t+1)​𝒃}.\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=t\bm{b}\}^{2}\geq\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=(t-1)\bm{b}\}\cdot\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=(t+1)\bm{b}\}.

∎

Remark 3.6.

We remark that if MM is unimodular and 𝒃∈ℤm,𝒌1,𝒌2∈ℤn\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} are given, the polytope ℬ(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(M,𝒃)\mathcal{B}_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(M,\bm{b}) is indeed IDP. However, not all IDP polytopes are obtained this way. Furthermore, Lemma 3.4 is not generally correct for an arbitrary IDP polytope. In particular, with the added assumption that MM has full row rank, one can show that MM is unimodular iff ℬ(𝒌1,𝒌2)​(𝒃)\mathcal{B}_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b}) has integral vertices for any choice of 𝒃,𝒌1,𝒌2\bm{b},\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2}. Thus, the proof of Theorem 3.1 does not extend to IDP polytopes. In fact, Corollary 3.5 fails for general IDP polytopes, see [22].

3.2 Solution Laurent polynomials of TU matrices

Suppose M∈{0,±1}m×nM\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{m\times n} is a totally unimodular matrix. For any 𝒃∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}, we want to find a lower bound for #⁡{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝒚=𝒃}\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}. We encode these quantities as coefficients of a Laurent polynomial and prove that this Laurent polynomial is VLC\LC. We will then use Proposition 2.2 to obtain lower bounds for its coefficients in Section 4.

Suppose 𝒂1,⋯,𝒂n∈ℤm\bm{a}_{1},\cdots,\bm{a}_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} are the columns of MM. For any integer vector 𝒌∈ℤ≥0n\bm{k}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}, define the 𝒌\bm{k}-solution Laurent polynomial of MM to be:

PM,𝒌(xi:i∈[m])=∏j=1n(∑ℓ=0kj𝒙ℓ​𝒂j)=∑𝒃∈ℤmB(𝟎,𝒌)(𝒃)𝒙𝒃,P_{M,\bm{k}}(x_{i}:i\in[m])=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{\ell=0}^{k_{j}}\bm{x}^{\ell\bm{a}_{j}}\right)=\sum_{\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}}B_{(\bm{0},\bm{k})}(\bm{b})\bm{x^{b}},

where B(𝒌1,𝒌2)(𝒃)=#{𝒚∈ℤn:M𝒚=𝒃,𝒌1≤𝒚≤𝒌2}B_{(\bm{k}_{1},\bm{k}_{2})}(\bm{b})=\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b},\bm{k}_{1}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}_{2}\}, as defined in Section 3.1.

The goal of this section is to prove that PM,𝒌P_{M,\bm{k}} is VLC\LC for any TU matrix MM and 𝒌∈ℤn\bm{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}. See Remark 3.9 on why we cannot prove a similar statement for unimodular matrices.

Let us first derive a simpler equivalent condition for PM,𝒌P_{M,\bm{k}} to be VLC\LC. For the sake of simplicity, if MM is an m×nm\times n matrix and S⊆[m]S\subseteq[m], we denote by MSM_{S} the submatrix of MM consisting of the rows indexed by SS.

Proposition 3.7.

Suppose MM is a TU matrix. Then PM,𝐤P_{M,\bm{k}} is VLC\LC if and only if the following condition holds:

Choose an arbitrary subset S⊆[m]S\subseteq[m] of the rows of MM. Let B=MSB=M_{S} and A=M[m]∖SA=M_{[m]\setminus S}. Further choose an arbitrary 𝐛∈ℤ|S|\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{|S|}. Then any positive evaluation of the Laurent polynomial ∑𝟎≤𝐲≤𝐤B​𝐲=b𝐱A​𝐲\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}\\ B\bm{y}=b\end{subarray}}\bm{x}^{A\bm{y}} in all but one variable has log-concave coefficients.

Proof.

By Definition 2.1, PM,𝒌P_{M,\bm{k}} is VLC\LC if for any S⊆[m]S\subseteq[m] and 𝒃∈ℤ|S|\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{|S|}, any positive evaluation of [𝒙S𝒃]​pM,𝒌[\bm{x}_{S}^{\bm{b}}]p_{M,\bm{k}} in all but one variable has log-concave coefficients. We can write:

[𝒙S𝒃]​pM,𝒌​(𝒙)\displaystyle[\bm{x}_{S}^{\bm{b}}]p_{M,\bm{k}}(\bm{x}) =[𝒙S𝒃]​∑𝟎≤𝒚≤𝒌𝒙M​𝒚\displaystyle=[\bm{x}_{S}^{\bm{b}}]\sum_{\bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}}\bm{x}^{M\bm{y}}
=∑𝟎≤𝒚≤𝒌B​𝒚=𝒃𝒙A​𝒚,\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}\\ B\bm{y}=\bm{b}\end{subarray}}\bm{x}^{A\bm{y}},

completing the proof. ∎

Proposition 3.7 already reveals the connection between VLC\LC properties of 𝒌\bm{k}-solution Laurent polynomials of TU matrices and midpoint log-concavity for TU polytopes. The following proposition completes this connection.

Proposition 3.8.

Suppose [AB]\begin{bmatrix}A\\ B\end{bmatrix} is a TU matrix and assume AA is an m×nm\times n matrix. Then any positive evaluation of ∑𝟎≤𝐲≤𝐤B​𝐲=b𝐱A​𝐲\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}\\ B\bm{y}=b\end{subarray}}\bm{x}^{A\bm{y}} in all but one variable has log-concave coefficients.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, evaluate ∑𝟎≤𝒚≤𝒌B​𝒚=b𝒙A​𝒚\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}\\ B\bm{y}=b\end{subarray}}\bm{x}^{A\bm{y}} in all but the last variable, and let q⁡(x)q(x) be the resulting Laurent polynomial. It remains to check that {[xβ]​q}β∈ℤ\{[x^{\beta}]q\}_{\beta\in\mathbb{Z}} is a log-concave sequence.

Let 𝒂(1),𝒂(2),⋯,𝒂(m)\bm{a}_{(1)},\bm{a}_{(2)},\cdots,\bm{a}_{(m)} be the rows of AA, and suppose we are evaluating pp at y1=r1,⋯,ym−1=rm−1y_{1}=r_{1},\cdots,y_{m-1}=r_{m-1}. Then:

Remark 3.9.

Suppose MM is a general unimodular matrix. To prove that PM,𝒌P_{M,\bm{k}} is VLC\LC, we need to show that ∑𝟎≤𝒚≤𝒌B​𝒚=b𝒙A​𝒚\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}\\ B\bm{y}=b\end{subarray}}\bm{x}^{A\bm{y}} is VLC\LC for every partition of the rows of MM into two submatrices AA and BB. However, the proof of Proposition 3.8 does not always for unimodular matrices since [B0Aiden+mT]\begin{bmatrix}B&0\\ A&\mathrm{id}\\ \lx@intercol\hfil e_{n+m}^{T}\hfil\lx@intercol\end{bmatrix} does not necessarily remain unimodular.

Corollary 3.10.

By Proposition 3.7 and Proposition 3.8, the 𝐤\bm{k}-solution Laurent polynomial of any TU matrix is VLC\LC for any 𝐤≥𝟎\bm{k}\geq\bm{0}.

4 Capacity bounds for lattice points of TU polytopes

With Corollary 3.10 at our disposal, we can use Proposition 2.2 to derive capacity bounds for B(𝟎,𝒌)​(M,𝒃)B_{(\bm{0},\bm{k})}(M,\bm{b}) based on cap𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}) and Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}). In this section, we will focus on finding explicit bounds for the set Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}) based on MM, 𝒃\bm{b} and 𝒌\bm{k}. We look at general TU matrices in Section 4.1 and find a simply exponential lower bound for B⁡(M,𝒃):=#⁡{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝒚=𝒃}B(M,\bm{b}):=\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}. In Section 4.2, we look at two special classes of TU matrices and find another lower bound for BM​(𝒃)B_{M}(\bm{b}).

First, let us find an alternate characterization for both min⁡Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\min\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}) and max⁡Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\max\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}) using LP strong duality. For any matrix M∈ℝm×nM\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, let 𝒎(i)\bm{m}_{(i)} be the ii-th row of MM and let M[i+1,m]M_{[i+1,m]} denote the submatrix of MM consisting of the rows i+1,⋯,mi+1,\cdots,m. Further define 𝒔i\bm{s}_{i} to be the sum of the first ii rows of MM. In particular, if 𝒃∈ℝm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} is a vector, then 𝒃[i+1,m]\bm{b}_{[i+1,m]} is the restriction of 𝒃\bm{b} to its i+1,⋯,mi+1,\cdots,m-th entries.

Proposition 4.1.

Let MM be an m×nm\times n TU matrix and 𝐤∈ℤn\bm{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}. For any i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1]:

maxDegi𝒃(PM,𝒌)=min{𝒃[i+1,m]T𝒘+𝒌T𝒛:(M[i+1,m])T𝒘+𝒛≥𝒎(i),𝒛≥𝟎},\max\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})=\min\{\bm{b}_{[i+1,m]}^{T}\bm{w}+\bm{k}^{T}\bm{z}:(M_{[i+1,m]})^{T}\bm{w}+\bm{z}\geq\bm{m}_{(i)},\,\bm{z}\geq\bm{0}\},

Similarly:

minDegi𝒃(PM,𝒌)=max{𝒃[i+1,m]T𝒘−𝒌T𝒛:(M[i+1,m])T𝒘−𝒛≤𝒎(i),𝒛≥𝟎}.\min\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})=\max\{\bm{b}_{[i+1,m]}^{T}\bm{w}-\bm{k}^{T}\bm{z}:(M_{[i+1,m]})^{T}\bm{w}-\bm{z}\leq\bm{m}_{(i)},\,\bm{z}\geq\bm{0}\}.
Proof.

The set of degrees of yiy_{i} in [yi+1αi+1⋯ymαm]PM,𝟎,𝒌[{y_{i+1}^{\alpha_{i+1}}}\cdots y_{m}^{\alpha_{m}}]P_{M,\bm{0},\bm{k}} is as follows:

Degi𝒃(PM,𝒌)={𝒎(i)T𝒙:M[i+1,m]𝒚=𝒃[i+1,m], 0≤𝒚≤𝒌,𝒚∈ℤn},\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})=\{\bm{m}_{(i)}^{T}\bm{x}:M_{[i+1,m]}\bm{y}=\bm{b}_{[i+1,m]},\,\bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k},\,\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}\},

since MM is a TU matrix, a tight upper bound for this set would be the solution to the LP problem:

max{𝒎(i)T𝒚:M[i+1,m]𝒚=b[i+1,m],𝟎≤𝒚≤𝒌}.\max\{\bm{m}_{(i)}^{T}\bm{y}:M_{[i+1,m]}\bm{y}=b_{[i+1,m]},\bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}\}.

The dual of this LP is:

min{𝒃[i+1,m]T𝒘+𝒌T𝒛:(M[i+1,m])T𝒘+𝒛≥𝒎(i),𝒛≥𝟎}.\min\{\bm{b}_{[i+1,m]}^{T}\bm{w}+\bm{k}^{T}\bm{z}:(M_{[i+1,m]})^{T}\bm{w}+\bm{z}\geq\bm{m}_{(i)},\bm{z}\geq\bm{0}\}.

By strong LP duality, the objective value of (P) and (D) are equal, completing the first part of the proof. The argument for min⁡Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\min\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}) is similar. ∎

Computing the optimal values of the LPs in Proposition 4.1 for all i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1] can be computationally costly. Instead, we evaluate the objective functions of these LPs at feasible points, getting weaker bounds for Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}). We can use this looser bound to obtain a capacity lower bound for B(𝟎,𝒌)​(M,𝒃)B_{(\bm{0},\bm{k})}(M,\bm{b}) by Proposition 2.2. We will look at two different sets of feasible points for these LPs. First, we will let 𝒘=𝟎\bm{w}=\bm{0} and adjust 𝒛\bm{z} accordingly to find a feasible point. This way we get capacity lower bounds for any TU matrix MM, which are stated in Section 4.1. Second, we will let 𝒛=𝟎\bm{z}=\bm{0} and adjust 𝒘\bm{w} accordingly. In case a feasible 𝒘\bm{w} exists, we can find an alternate capacity lower bound for B(𝟎,𝒌)​(M,𝒃)B_{(\bm{0},\bm{k})}(M,\bm{b}), see Section 4.2. In particular, we find a lower bound for B(𝟎,𝒌)​(M,𝒃)B_{(\bm{0},\bm{k})}(M,\bm{b}) when MM has non-negative partial row sums and recover a lower bound for the number of lattice points of a flow polytope already presented in [36] and [35].

4.1 General capacity bounds for TU polytopes

As proven in Corollary 3.10, the 𝒌\bm{k}-solution Laurent polynomial of any TU matrix is VLC\LC. Thus we can obtain a lower bound for B(𝟎,𝒌)​(M,𝒃)B_{(\bm{0},\bm{k})}(M,\bm{b}) using Proposition 2.2:

Theorem 4.2.

For any m×nm\times n TU matrix MM and any integer vectors 𝐤∈ℤn\bm{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}, 𝐛∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} we have:

B(𝟎,𝒌)​(M,𝒃)≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)⋅∏i=1mmax⁡{|αi−bi||αi−bi|(1+|αi−bi|)1+|αi−bi|,|γi−bi||γi−bi|(1+|γi−bi|)1+|γi−bi|},B_{(\bm{0},\bm{k})}(M,\bm{b})\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}\max\left\{\frac{|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|^{|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|}}{(1+|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|)^{1+|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|}},\frac{|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|^{|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|}}{(1+|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|)^{1+|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|}}\right\},

where:

αi=−∑j∈[n]:Mi,j=−1kj,γi=∑j∈[n]:Mi,j=1kj∀i∈[m].\alpha_{i}=-\sum_{j\in[n]:M_{i,j}=-1}k_{j},\quad\gamma_{i}=\sum_{j\in[n]:M_{i,j}=1}k_{j}\quad\forall i\in[m].
Proof.

It follows from Proposition 2.2 that:

B(𝟎,𝒌)​(M,𝒃)≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)⋅∏i=1m|βi−bi||βi−bi|(1+|βi−bi|)1+|βi−bi|,B_{(\bm{0},\bm{k})}(M,\bm{b})\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}\frac{|\beta_{i}-b_{i}|^{|\beta_{i}-b_{i}|}}{(1+|\beta_{i}-b_{i}|)^{1+|\beta_{i}-b_{i}|}},

where βi\beta_{i} is either a lower bound or an upper bound Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}). Recall that for any r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R}:

(r)+={r if ​r>00 otherwiseand(r)−={r if ​r<00 otherwise,(r)_{+}=\begin{cases}r&\text{ if }r>0\\ 0&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases}\quad\text{and}\quad(r)_{-}=\begin{cases}r&\text{ if }r<0\\ 0&\text{ otherwise}\end{cases},

and for any vector 𝒗∈ℝn\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, both (𝒗)+(\bm{v})_{+}, (𝒗)−(\bm{v})_{-} are applied coordinate-wise. It is easy to check that the pair 𝒘=𝟎,𝒛=(𝒎(i))+\bm{w}=\bm{0},\bm{z}=(\bm{m}_{(i)})_{+} satisfy (M[i+1,m])T​𝒘+𝒛≥𝒎(i),𝒛≥𝟎(M_{[i+1,m]})^{T}\bm{w}+\bm{z}\geq\bm{m}_{(i)},\bm{z}\geq\bm{0}. It follows from Proposition 4.1 that γi\gamma_{i} is indeed an upper bound for Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}) for any i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1]. Similarly, 𝒘=𝟎,𝒛=−(𝒎(i))−\bm{w}=\bm{0},\bm{z}=-(\bm{m}_{(i)})_{-} is a feasible point for (M[i+1,m])T​𝒘−𝒛≤𝒎(i),𝒛≥𝟎(M_{[i+1,m]})^{T}\bm{w}-\bm{z}\leq\bm{m}_{(i)},\bm{z}\geq\bm{0}, implying that αi\alpha_{i} is a lower bound for Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}) for any i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1].

It is also easy to check that αm,γm\alpha_{m},\gamma_{m} are bounds for Degm𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\Deg_{m}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}), since:

−∑j∈[n]:Mm,j=−1kj≤∑j∈[n]Mm,jxj≤∑j∈[n]:Mm,j=1kj,∀𝟎≤𝒙≤𝒌-\sum_{j\in[n]:M_{m,j}=-1}k_{j}\leq\sum_{j\in[n]}M_{m,j}x_{j}\leq\sum_{j\in[n]:M_{m,j}=1}k_{j},\quad\forall\bm{0}\leq\bm{x}\leq\bm{k}

Hence proving the statement. ∎

Let us assume that the fiber {𝒚∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝒚=𝒃}\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\} is finite. Then there should exist some 𝒌\bm{k} such that any 𝒚\bm{y} in this fiber satisfies 𝒚≤𝒌\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}. For such a 𝒌\bm{k}, the bound of Theorem 4.2 becomes a bound for B⁡(M,𝒃)=#⁡{𝒚∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝒚=𝒃}B(M,\bm{b})=\#\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}. Through the rest of this section, we will explore the properties of TU matrices MM with finite fibers and prove capacity bounds for B⁡(M,𝒃)B(M,\bm{b}).

Lemma 4.3.

Suppose MM is an m×nm\times n TU matrix and the fiber {𝐲∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝐲=𝐛}\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\} is nonempty and finite for some integer vector 𝐛\bm{b}. Then any point of this fiber satisfies yi≤‖𝐛‖1y_{i}\leq\|\bm{b}\|_{1} for any i∈[n]i\in[n].

Proof.

In fact, we can prove that any point 𝒚\bm{y} of P={𝒚:M𝒚=𝒃,𝒚≥𝟎}P=\{\bm{y}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b},\bm{y}\geq\bm{0}\} satisfies yi≤‖𝒃‖1y_{i}\leq\|\bm{b}\|_{1}.

We know that the polyhedron PP is bounded since MM is TU and {𝒚∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝒚=𝒃}\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\} is finite. So PP is the convex hull of its vertices and by convexity, it suffices to show that any vertex 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*} of {𝒚:M𝒚=𝒃,𝒚≥𝟎}\{\bm{y}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b},\bm{y}\geq\bm{0}\} satisfies yi≤‖𝒃‖1y_{i}\leq\|\bm{b}\|_{1}.

Let r=rank⁡(M)r=\rank(M) and let 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*} be a vertex of PP. The columns of MM indexed by supp⁡(𝒚∗):={i∈[n]:yi∗≠0}\supp(\bm{y}^{*}):=\{i\in[n]:y^{*}_{i}\neq 0\} are linearly independent. Otherwise, there would exist a nonzero vector 𝒗\bm{v} supported on supp⁡(𝒚∗)\supp(\bm{y}^{*}) with M​𝒗=0M\bm{v}=0, so that 𝒚∗±ε​𝒗∈P\bm{y}^{*}\pm\varepsilon\bm{v}\in P for sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0, contradicting the fact that 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*} is a vertex.

Let BB be a set of rr linearly independent columns of MM containing supp⁡(𝒚∗)\supp(\bm{y}^{*}) ( BB is also known as the basis of vertex 𝒚∗\bm{y}^{*} in linear programming). Then yi=0y_{i}=0 for i∉Bi\notin B. Let M:,BM_{:,B} be the submatrix of MM containing the columns indexed by BB. M:,BM_{:,B} still has rank rr, so choose a R⊆[m]R\subseteq[m] with |R|=r|R|=r such that the submatrix of M:,BM_{:,B} containing the rows indexed by RR is invertible. Let this r×rr\times r submatrix be MR,BM_{R,B}.

Restricting M​𝒚∗=𝒃M\bm{y}^{*}=\bm{b} to the rows in RR and columns in BB gives us that MR,B​𝒚B∗=𝒃rM_{R,B}\bm{y}^{*}_{B}=\bm{b}_{r}, thus 𝒚B=MR,B−1​𝒃R.\bm{y}_{B}=M_{R,B}^{-1}\bm{b}_{R}. Since MM is TU, MR,B−1M_{R,B}^{-1} is TU as well, and any entry of MR,B−1M_{R,B}^{-1} belongs to {0,±1}\{0,\pm 1\}. Consequently, for each i∈Bi\in B we have:

yi≤∑j∈R|bj|≤‖𝒃‖1.y_{i}\leq\sum_{j\in R}|b_{j}|\leq\|\bm{b}\|_{1}.

The same bound holds for i∉Bi\notin B because yi=0y_{i}=0. ∎

Corollary 4.4.

Suppose M∈{0,±1}m×nM\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{m\times n} is a TU matrix. Let r=rank⁡(M)r=\rank(M) and c=‖b‖1c=\|b\|_{1}. Then:

B⁡(M,𝒃)≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,c⋅𝟏)⋅∏i=1mmax⁡{|αi−bi||αi−bi|(1+|αi−bi|)1+|αi−bi|,|γi−bi||γi−bi|(1+|γi−bi|)1+|γi−bi|},B(M,\bm{b})\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,c\cdot\bm{1}})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}\max\left\{\frac{|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|^{|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|}}{(1+|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|)^{1+|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|}},\frac{|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|^{|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|}}{(1+|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|)^{1+|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|}}\right\},

where

αi=−c⋅(# of (-1)s in row i),γi=c⋅(# of (+1)s in row i)∀i∈[m].\alpha_{i}=-c\cdot(\#\text{ of (-1)s in row }i),\quad\gamma_{i}=c\cdot(\#\text{ of (+1)s in row }i)\quad\forall i\in[m].
Proof.

The bound is trivial if B⁡(M,𝒃)B(M,\bm{b}) is not finite. Otherwise, by Lemma 4.3 B⁡(M,𝒃)=B𝟎,c⋅𝟏​(M,𝒃)B(M,\bm{b})=B_{\bm{0},c\cdot\bm{1}}(M,\bm{b}). The result follows from Theorem 4.2. ∎

We can further simplify the lower bound of Corollary 4.4 to obtain a simply exponential lower bound for B⁡(M,𝒃)B(M,\bm{b}) for large enough integer vectors 𝒃\bm{b}.

Corollary 4.5.

Suppose M∈{0,±1}m×nM\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{m\times n} is a TU matrix with finite fibers. Then:

B⁡(M,𝒃)≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,‖b‖1⋅𝟏)⋅exp⁡(−m−m​log⁡(1+n​∥𝒃∥1))B(M,\bm{b})\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}\left(P_{M,\|b\|_{1}\cdot\bm{1}}\right)\cdot\exp\left(-m-m\log(1+n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1})\right)
Proof.

By Corollary 4.4 with c=∥𝒃∥1c=\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}:

B⁡(M,𝒃)≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,c⋅𝟏)⋅∏i=1mmax⁡{|αi−bi||αi−bi|(1+|αi−bi|)1+|αi−bi|,|γi−bi||γi−bi|(1+|γi−bi|)1+|γi−bi|},B(M,\bm{b})\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,c\cdot\bm{1}})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}\max\left\{\frac{|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|^{|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|}}{(1+|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|)^{1+|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|}},\frac{|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|^{|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|}}{(1+|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|)^{1+|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|}}\right\},

where:

αi=−c⋅(# of (-1)s in row i),γi=c⋅(# of (+1)s in row i)∀i∈[m].\alpha_{i}=-c\cdot(\#\text{ of (-1)s in row }i),\quad\gamma_{i}=c\cdot(\#\text{ of (+1)s in row }i)\quad\forall i\in[m].

Note that γi≤n​c\gamma_{i}\leq nc and −n​c≤αi-nc\leq\alpha_{i}. Furthermore, z↦zz(1+z)1+zz\mapsto\frac{z^{z}}{(1+z)^{1+z}} is a decreasing function over ℝ>0\mathbb{R}_{>0}. Thus:

B⁡(M,𝒃)\displaystyle B(M,\bm{b}) ≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,c⋅𝟏)⋅∏i=1mmax⁡{|αi−bi||αi−bi|(1+|αi−bi|)1+|αi−bi|,|γi−bi||γi−bi|(1+|γi−bi|)1+|γi−bi|}\displaystyle\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,c\cdot\bm{1}})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}\max\left\{\frac{|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|^{|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|}}{(1+|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|)^{1+|\alpha_{i}-b_{i}|}},\frac{|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|^{|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|}}{(1+|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|)^{1+|\gamma_{i}-b_{i}|}}\right\}
≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,c⋅𝟏)⋅∏i=1m|sgn⁡(bi)​n​c−bi||sgn⁡(bi)​n​c−bi|(1+|sgn⁡(bi)​n​c−bi|)1+|sgn⁡(bi)​n​c−bi|\displaystyle\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,c\cdot\bm{1}})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}\frac{|\sgn(b_{i})nc-b_{i}|^{|\sgn(b_{i})nc-b_{i}|}}{(1+|\sgn(b_{i})nc-b_{i}|)^{1+|\sgn(b_{i})nc-b_{i}|}}
≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,c⋅𝟏)⋅∏i=1m(n​∥𝒃∥1)n​∥𝒃∥1(1+|n​∥𝒃∥1|)1+n​∥𝒃∥1,\displaystyle\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,c\cdot\bm{1}})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}\frac{(n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1})^{n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}}}{(1+|n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}|)^{1+n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}}},

where sgn⁡(r)=1\sgn(r)=1 if r>0r>0 and sgn⁡(r)=−1\sgn(r)=-1 otherwise. Using the inequality kk(1+k)1+k≥1e⁡(1+k)\frac{k^{k}}{(1+k)^{1+k}}\geq\frac{1}{e(1+k)} for k>0k>0 we obtain:

B⁡(M,𝒃)\displaystyle B(M,\bm{b}) ≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,c⋅𝟏)⋅∏i=1m(n​∥𝒃∥1)n​∥𝒃∥1(1+n​∥𝒃∥1)1+n​∥𝒃∥1\displaystyle\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,c\cdot\bm{1}})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}\frac{(n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1})^{n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}}}{(1+n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1})^{1+n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}}}
≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,c⋅𝟏)⋅∏i=1mexp⁡(−1−log⁡(1+n​∥𝒃∥1))\displaystyle\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,c\cdot\bm{1}})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m}\exp({-1-\log(1+n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}))}
=cap𝒃⁡(PM,c⋅𝟏)⋅exp⁡(−m−m​log⁡(1+n​∥𝒃∥1)).\displaystyle=\cpc_{\bm{b}}\left(P_{M,c\cdot\bm{1}}\right)\cdot\exp\left(-m-m\log(1+n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1})\right).

∎

If ∥𝒃∥1\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1} is reasonably large so that m+m​log⁡(1+n​∥𝒃∥1)=O⁡(∥𝒃∥1)m+m\log(1+n\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1})=O(\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}), one could rewrite the bound of Corollary 4.5 as a simply exponential bound in ∥𝒃∥1\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}. The following corollary establishes a bound for ∥𝒃∥1\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1} that gives us such a simply exponential bound for B⁡(M,𝒃)B(M,\bm{b}).

Corollary 4.6.

Suppose m,nm,n are positive integers satisfying max⁡{m,n}≥3\max\{m,n\}\geq 3. Given a TU matrix M∈{0,±1}m×nM\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{m\times n} with finite fibers and some 𝐛∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} satisfying ∥𝐛∥1≥6​m⋅log⁡(max⁡{m,n})\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}\geq 6m\cdot\log(\max\{m,n\}), we have:

B⁡(M,𝒃)≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,∥𝒃∥1⋅𝟏)⋅exp⁡(−∥𝒃∥1)B(M,\bm{b})\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}\cdot\bm{1}})\cdot\exp\left(-\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}\right)
Proof.

Apply Corollary 4.5 to MM and 𝒃\bm{b}. We just have to check that:

∥𝒃∥1≥m+m​log⁡(1+n​∥b∥1),\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}\geq m+m\log(1+n\lVert b\rVert_{1}),

or the following stronger inequality:

∥𝒃∥1−m​log⁡(∥𝒃∥1)≥m+m​log⁡(2)+m​log⁡(n)\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}-m\log(\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1})\geq m+m\log(2)+m\log(n)

The function z↦z−m​log⁡(z)z\mapsto z-m\log(z) is increasing for z>mz>m, therefore it suffices to check the above inequality for ∥𝒃∥1=6​m⋅log⁡(q)\lVert\bm{b}\rVert_{1}=6m\cdot\log(q) where q=max⁡{m,n}q=\max\{m,n\}. Now we only need to show that:

6​log⁡q≥1+log⁡(2)+log⁡(q)+log⁡(6​q​log​q),6\log q\geq 1+\log(2)+\log(q)+\log(6q\log q),

or equivalently that 5​log⁡q≥1+log⁡(2)+log⁡(6​q​log⁡q)5\log q\geq 1+\log(2)+\log(6q\log q). Exponentiate both hand sides of this inequality to get the equivalent statement q4≥12​e​log⁡qq^{4}\geq 12e\log q, which holds for any q≥3q\geq 3. ∎

4.2 Special cases: non-negative partial row sums

In Section 4.1, we employed capacity bounds for VLC\LC polynomials stated in Proposition 2.2 alongside the dual characterization of max⁡Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\max\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}) and Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}) to find capacity bounds for B⁡(M,𝒃)B(M,\bm{b}) when MM is a general TU matrix. Specifically, we use feasible points with 𝒘=𝟎\bm{w}=\bm{0} for the dual LPs of Proposition 4.1.

In this section, rather than placing all of the weight of the choice of the feasible points on 𝒛\bm{z} by taking 𝒘=𝟎\bm{w}=\bm{0}, we will instead let 𝒛=𝟎∈ℤn\bm{z}=\bm{0}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} and search for a feasible 𝒘∈ℝm−i\bm{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{m-i}. This will not be always possible, however if that MM has non-negative partial row sums and the sum of all of its rows is the 𝟎\bm{0} vector, such a 𝒘\bm{w} always exists. In this case, we obtain a lower bound for B⁡(M,𝒃)B(M,\bm{b}) stated in Corollary 4.12. We can slightly improve this bound when MM is the incidence matrix of a directed acyclic graph to recover [35, Theorem 1.1], see Corollary 4.13. Lastly, we will state a lower bound for B⁡(M,𝒃)B(M,\bm{b}) when MM is a TU matrix with non-negative partial row sums in Corollary 4.14.

Theorem 4.7.

Suppose M∈{0,±1}m×nM\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{m\times n} and is a TU matrix and 𝐤∈ℤn\bm{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}. Let 𝐬i=𝐦(1)+⋯+𝐦(i)\bm{s}_{i}=\bm{m}_{(1)}+\cdots+\bm{m}_{(i)} be the sum of the first ii rows of MM for i∈[m]i\in[m]. Assume that 𝐬i≥𝟎\bm{s}_{i}\geq\bm{0} for any i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1] and 𝐬m=𝟎\bm{s}_{m}=\bm{0}. Then :

B(𝟎,𝒌)​(M,𝒃)≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)⋅∏i=1m−1|σi||σi|(1+|σi|)1+|σi|.B_{(\bm{0},\bm{k})}(M,\bm{b})\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\frac{|\sigma_{i}|^{|\sigma_{i}|}}{(1+|\sigma_{i}|)^{1+|\sigma_{i}|}}.

where σi=b1+⋯+bi\sigma_{i}=b_{1}+\cdots+b_{i} for i∈[m]i\in[m].

Proof.

If 𝒃∉supp⁡(PM,𝒌)\bm{b}\not\in\supp(P_{M,\bm{k}}), then cap𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)=0\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})=0 by Proposition 2.4 and Fact 2.5, and the statement is trivial. Otherwise if there exists 𝟎≤𝒚≤𝒌\bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k} satisfying M​𝒚=𝒃M\bm{y}=\bm{b}, we should have σm=0\sigma_{m}=0 since 𝒔m=𝟎\bm{s}_{m}=\bm{0}.

Let i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1]. Since 𝒎(i)+⋯+𝒎(m)=𝒔m−𝒔i−1≤𝟎\bm{m}_{(i)}+\cdots+\bm{m}_{(m)}=\bm{s}_{m}-\bm{s}_{i-1}\leq\bm{0} , the vector 𝒘=−𝟏∈ℤm−i\bm{w}=-\bm{1}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m-i} satisfies:

(M[i+1,m])T​𝒘≥𝒎(i).(M_{[i+1,m]})^{T}\bm{w}\geq\bm{m}_{(i)}.

So −𝒃[i+1,m]T​𝟏=σi−σm=σi-\bm{b}_{[i+1,m]}^{T}\bm{1}=\sigma_{i}-\sigma_{m}=\sigma_{i} is an upper bound for the set Degi𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)\Deg_{i}^{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}}) by Proposition 4.1. Moreover, 𝒎(m)=−𝒔(m−1)≤𝟎\bm{m}_{(m)}=-\bm{s}_{(m-1)}\leq\bm{0}, thus 00 is an upper bound for the set of degrees of xmx_{m} appearing in PM,𝒌​(𝒙)P_{M,\bm{k}}(\bm{x}). By Proposition 2.2, we get:

B(𝟎,𝒌)​(M,𝒃)\displaystyle B_{(\bm{0},\bm{k})}(M,\bm{b}) ≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)⋅|−bm||−bm|(1+|−bm|)1+|−bm|⋅∏i=1m−1|σi−bi||σi−bi|(1+|σi−bi|)1+|σi−bi|\displaystyle\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})\cdot\frac{|-b_{m}|^{|-b_{m}|}}{(1+|-b_{m}|)^{1+|-b_{m}|}}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\frac{|\sigma_{i}-b_{i}|^{|\sigma_{i}-b_{i}|}}{(1+|\sigma_{i}-b_{i}|)^{1+|\sigma_{i}-b_{i}|}}
=cap𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)⋅|σm−1||σm−1|(1+|σm−1|)1+|σm−1|⋅∏i=1m−2|σi||σi|(1+|σi|)1+|σi|\displaystyle=\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})\cdot\frac{|\sigma_{m-1}|^{|\sigma_{m-1}|}}{(1+|\sigma_{m-1}|)^{1+|\sigma_{m-1}|}}\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m-2}\frac{|\sigma_{i}|^{|\sigma_{i}|}}{(1+|\sigma_{i}|)^{1+|\sigma_{i}|}}
=cap𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)⋅∏i=1m−1|σi||σi|(1+|σi|)1+|σi|,\displaystyle=\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\frac{|\sigma_{i}|^{|\sigma_{i}|}}{(1+|\sigma_{i}|)^{1+|\sigma_{i}|}},

proving the desired bound. ∎

We can apply Theorem 4.7 with a large enough 𝒌\bm{k} to bound B⁡(M,𝒃)B(M,\bm{b}). In fact, we can take the limit of the bound of Theorem 4.7 as 𝒌→∞\bm{k}\to\infty, by which we mean that every entry of 𝒌\bm{k} tends to infinity. If the lower bound converges as 𝒌→∞\bm{k}\to\infty, we get a bound for B⁡(M,𝒃)B(M,\bm{b}).

Lemma 4.8.

Suppose MM is an m×nm\times n TU matrix such that 𝐬i≥𝟎\bm{s}_{i}\geq\bm{0} for any i∈[m]i\in[m]. If MM does not have an all zeros column, then all the fibers {𝐲∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝐲=𝐛}\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\} are finite.

Proof.

Suppose not, and let {𝒚∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝒚=𝒃}\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\} be infinite. Then by Dickson’s lemma, there exists two distinct integer vectors 𝒛≥𝒚\bm{z}\geq\bm{y} satisfying M​𝒚=M​𝒛=𝒃M\bm{y}=M\bm{z}=\bm{b}. Thus, there exists some nonzero vector 𝒗∈ℝ≥0n\bm{v}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n} satisfying M​𝒗=𝟎M\bm{v}=\bm{0}. Let j∈[n]j\in[n] be an index such that vj>0v_{j}>0. We have:

[𝟏i𝟎m−i]T​M​𝒗=𝒔(i)T​𝒗=0,∀i∈[m]\begin{bmatrix}\bm{1}_{i}\\ \bm{0}_{m-i}\end{bmatrix}^{T}M\bm{v}=\bm{s}_{(i)}^{T}\bm{v}=0,\quad\forall i\in[m]

where 𝟏i∈ℤi\bm{1}_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}^{i} is the all ones vector and 𝟎m−i∈ℤm−i\bm{0}_{m-i}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m-i} the all zeros vector. Note that 𝒔(i),𝒗≥𝟎\bm{s}_{(i)},\bm{v}\geq\bm{0}, so we must have 𝒔(i),j=0\bm{s}_{(i),j}=0 for any i∈[m]i\in[m]. That is:

𝒔(1),j=𝒔(2),j=⋯=𝒔(m),j,\bm{s}_{(1),j}=\bm{s}_{(2),j}=\cdots=\bm{s}_{(m),j},

which means that the jj-th column of MM is a zero column, contradicting our assumption. ∎

Similar to the terminology of [35], for a Laurent series f⁡(𝒙)f(\bm{x}) with non-negative coefficients, we define its domain of convergence as Ωf={𝒙>𝟎:f⁡(𝒙)​ converges }\Omega_{f}=\{\bm{x}>\bm{0}:f(\bm{x})\text{ converges }\}, and define its capacity as cap𝜶⁡(f)=inf𝒙∈Ωff⁡(𝒙)𝒙𝜶\cpc_{\bm{\alpha}}(f)=\inf_{\bm{x}\in\Omega_{f}}\frac{f(\bm{x})}{\bm{x}^{\bm{\alpha}}}. If we define 𝒇⁡(𝒙)=∞\bm{f}(\bm{x})=\infty for any 𝒙∉Ωf\bm{x}\not\in\Omega_{f}, this definition of capacity agrees with the earlier definition cap𝜶⁡(f)=inf𝒙>𝟎f⁡(𝒙)𝒙𝜶\cpc_{\bm{\alpha}}(f)=\inf_{\bm{x}>\bm{0}}\frac{f(\bm{x})}{\bm{x}^{\bm{\alpha}}}.

Let 𝒂1,⋯,𝒂n\bm{a}_{1},\cdots,\bm{a}_{n} be the columns of MM and define:

PM​(𝒚):=∑𝒚≥𝟎𝒙M​𝒚=∏j=1n∑ℓ≥0𝒙ℓ​𝒂j.P_{M}(\bm{y}):=\sum_{\bm{y}\geq\bm{0}}\bm{x}^{M\bm{y}}=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell\geq 0}\bm{x}^{\ell\bm{a}_{j}}.

Suppose MM is an m×nm\times n TU matrix and has finite fibers, i.e. {𝒚∈ℤ≥0n:M​𝒚=𝒃}\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\} is finite for any 𝒃∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}. This holds, for example, when MM has non-negative partial row sums and no zero columns (see Lemma 4.8). Then PMP_{M} is a well defined Laurent series with the domain of convergence Ω={𝒙∈ℝ>0m:𝒙𝒂j<1∀j∈[n]}\Omega=\{\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}_{>0}:\bm{x}^{\bm{a}_{j}}<1\quad\forall j\in[n]\}. Moreover, Ω\Omega is a nonempty set. By Motzkin’s transposition theorem [25, Theorem 7.17], there exists some 𝒘\bm{w} such that 𝒘T​𝒂j>0\bm{w}^{T}\bm{a}_{j}>0 for any j∈[n]j\in[n] since MM has finite fibers. It follows that e−r​𝒘∈Ωe^{-r\bm{w}}\in\Omega for any r>0r>0. More precisely, the domain of convergence of each ∑ℓ≥0𝒙ℓ​𝒂j\sum_{\ell\geq 0}\bm{x}^{\ell\bm{a}_{j}} is open and contains e−r​𝒘e^{-r\bm{w}}.

Lemma 4.9 ([35, Proposition 6.4] ).

Suppose f1​(𝐱),⋯,fn​(𝐱)f_{1}(\bm{x}),\cdots,f_{n}(\bm{x}) are all Laurent series with non-negative coefficients. Let Ωi≠∅\Omega_{i}\neq\emptyset be the domain of convergence of fif_{i}, and suppose ∩i=1nintΩi≠∅\cap_{i=1}^{n}\innt\Omega_{i}\neq\emptyset. Then:

cap𝜶⁡(∏i=1nfi)=sup𝜶(1)+⋯+α(n)=𝜶∏i=1ncap𝜶(i)⁡(fi).\cpc_{\bm{\alpha}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}f_{i}\right)=\sup_{\bm{\alpha}_{(1)}+\cdots+\alpha_{(n)}=\bm{\alpha}}\prod_{i=1}^{n}\cpc_{\bm{\alpha}_{(i)}}(f_{i}).

In fact, after taking the natural logarithm of both hand sides, the two programs are Fenchel primal-dual.

In our case, this implies a particularly nice expression for the capacity of PMP_{M}. We can also obtain a conceptually similar expression for the capacity of PM,𝒌P_{M,\bm{k}}, which we discuss below.

Corollary 4.10.

Fix an m×nm\times n TU matrix MM with finite fibers and an integer vector 𝐛∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}. Letting ℬ⁡(M,𝐛)={𝐲∈ℝ≥0n:M​𝐲=𝐛}\mathcal{B}{(M,\bm{b})}=\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b}\}, we have

cap𝒃⁡(PM)=sup𝒔∈ℬ⁡(M,𝒃)∏j=1n(sj+1)sj+1sjsj.\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M})=\sup_{\bm{s}\in\mathcal{B}{(M,\bm{b})}}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{(s_{j}+1)^{s_{j}+1}}{s_{j}^{s_{j}}}.
Proof.

Let 𝒂1,⋯,𝒂n∈ℤm\bm{a}_{1},\cdots,\bm{a}_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} be the columns of MM. By Lemma 4.9 we can write:

cap𝒃⁡(PM)=sup𝒃1+⋯+𝒃n=𝒃∏j=1ncap𝒃j⁡(∑ℓ≥0𝒙ℓ​𝒂j).\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M})=\sup_{\bm{b}_{1}+\cdots+\bm{b}_{n}=\bm{b}}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\cpc_{\bm{b}_{j}}\left(\sum_{\ell\geq 0}\bm{x}^{\ell\bm{a}_{j}}\right).

We can further restrict to the case where 𝒃j\bm{b}_{j} is a non-negative multiple of 𝒂j\bm{a}_{j} by Fact 2.5, otherwise, cap𝒃j⁡(∑ℓ≥0𝒙ℓ​𝒂j)=0\cpc_{\bm{b}_{j}}\left(\sum_{\ell\geq 0}\bm{x}^{\ell\bm{a}_{j}}\right)=0. It follows that:

cap𝒃⁡(PM)=sup𝒔∈ℬ⁡(M,𝒃)∏j=1ncapsj​𝒂j⁡(∑ℓ≥0𝒙ℓ​𝒂j).\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M})=\sup_{\bm{s}\in\mathcal{B}(M,\bm{b})}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\cpc_{s_{j}\bm{a}_{j}}\left(\sum_{\ell\geq 0}\bm{x}^{\ell\bm{a}_{j}}\right).

One can see that capsj​𝒂j⁡(∑ℓ≥0𝒙ℓ​𝒂j)=cap𝒔j⁡(∑ℓ≥0xℓ)\cpc_{s_{j}\bm{a}_{j}}\left(\sum_{\ell\geq 0}\bm{x}^{\ell\bm{a}_{j}}\right)=\cpc_{\bm{s}_{j}}\left(\sum_{\ell\geq 0}x^{\ell}\right) by a change of variables. We further have capsj⁡(∑ℓ≥0xℓ)=(sj+1)sj+1sjsj\cpc_{s_{j}}\left(\sum_{\ell\geq 0}x^{\ell}\right)=\frac{(s_{j}+1)^{s_{j}+1}}{s_{j}^{s_{j}}} by [35, Example 4.16], completing the proof. ∎

We note that there is a similar expression for Corollary 4.10 in the case of the polytope ℬ𝟎,𝒌(M,𝒃)={𝒚∈ℝn:M𝒚=𝒃, 0≤𝒚≤𝒌}\mathcal{B}_{\bm{0},\bm{k}}{(M,\bm{b})}=\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b},\,\bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}\}. In that case, the capacity of PM,𝒌P_{M,\bm{k}} is the sup\sup over 𝒔∈ℬ𝟎,𝒌​(M,𝒃)\bm{s}\in\mathcal{B}_{\bm{0},\bm{k}}{(M,\bm{b})} of the product of eℋ{0,…,kj}​(sj)e^{\mathcal{H}_{\{0,\ldots,k_{j}\}}(s_{j})}, where ℋ{0,…,kj}​(sj)\mathcal{H}_{\{0,\ldots,k_{j}\}}(s_{j}) is the entropy of the entropy-maximizing distribution on {0,…,kj}\{0,\ldots,k_{j}\} with expectation sjs_{j} (Note that this is precisely what is given in Corollary 4.10, for the geometric distribution on ℤ≥0\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} with expectation sjs_{j}.)

Now we can use Lemma 4.9 to prove that capacity is continuous under limiting 𝒌→∞\bm{k}\to\infty.

Lemma 4.11.

Let MM be an m×nm\times n TU matrix with finite fibers and fix 𝐛∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m}. Then:

lim𝒌→∞cap𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)=cap𝒃⁡PM.\lim_{\bm{k}\to\infty}\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})=\cpc_{\bm{b}}P_{M}.
Proof.

Using Lemma 4.11, we conclude the following corollary:

Corollary 4.12.

Suppose M∈{0,±1}m×nM\in\{0,\pm 1\}^{m\times n} is a TU matrix with no zero columns and 𝐤∈ℤn\bm{k}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}. Let 𝐬i=𝐦(1)+⋯+𝐦(i)\bm{s}_{i}=\bm{m}_{(1)}+\cdots+\bm{m}_{(i)} be the sum of the first ii rows of MM for i∈[m]i\in[m]. Assume that 𝐬i≥𝟎\bm{s}_{i}\geq\bm{0} for any i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1] and 𝐬m=𝟎\bm{s}_{m}=\bm{0}. Then :

B⁡(M,𝒃)≥cap𝒃⁡(PM)⋅∏i=1m−1|σi||σi|(1+|σi|)1+|σi|.B(M,\bm{b})\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M})\cdot\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\frac{|\sigma_{i}|^{|\sigma_{i}|}}{(1+|\sigma_{i}|)^{1+|\sigma_{i}|}}.

where σi=b1+⋯+bi\sigma_{i}=b_{1}+\cdots+b_{i} for i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1].

We remark that we took a different approach in Section 4.1 when working with general TU matrices. This is because it is not clear whether the lower bound of Theorem 4.2 converges as 𝒌→∞\bm{k}\to\infty, or if it converges, whether it converges to a non-zero number.

We will explore two applications of Corollary 4.12. We will apply it to incidence matrices of directed acyclic graphs, and to TU matrices with non-negative partial row sums.

When MM is the incidence matrix of a directed acyclic graph GG, B⁡(M,𝒃)B(M,\bm{b}) is called the Kostant partition function for integer flows of GG. We refer to [32] for a more extensive study of these quantities. The following is not a direct corollary of Corollary 4.12, but follows the same steps with a slightly different choice of feasible points for Proposition 4.1.

Corollary 4.13 ([35, Theorem 1.1], see also [36]).

Let G=([n],E)G=([n],E) be a directed acyclic graph with edges directed from the larger to the smaller vertex. For each i∈[n]i\in[n], let GiG_{i} be the undirected induced subgraph of GG on vertices [i,n][i,n], and denote by CiC_{i} the connected component of ii in GiG_{i}. Then:

When GG is a directed acyclic graph with edges being directed from the larger vertices to smaller vertices, its incidence graph MM has non-negative partial row sums and the sum of all its rows is the zero vector. In fact, for each i∈[n]i\in[n], since there are no edges going into CiC_{i}, we have ∑j∈Ci𝒎(j)≤𝟎\sum_{j\in C_{i}}\bm{m}_{(j)}\leq\bm{0}, that is:

−(M[i+1,n])T𝟏Ci∖{i}=−∑j∈Ci∖{i}𝒎(j)≥𝒎(i),-(M_{[i+1,n]})^{T}\bm{1}_{C_{i}\setminus\{i\}}=-\sum_{j\in C_{i}\setminus\{i\}}\bm{m}_{(j)}\geq\bm{m}_{(i)},

where 𝟏Ci∖{i}\bm{1}_{C_{i}\setminus\{i\}} is the indicator vector of the set 𝑪𝒊∖{i}\bm{C_{i}}\setminus\{i\}. Similar to Theorem 4.7 and by Proposition 2.2, we get:

B(𝟎,𝒌)​(M,𝒃)≥cap𝒃⁡(PM,𝒌)⋅∏i=2n|σi||σi|(1+|σi|)1+|σi|,B_{(\bm{0},\bm{k})}(M,\bm{b})\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M,\bm{k}})\cdot\prod_{i=2}^{n}\frac{|\sigma_{i}|^{|\sigma_{i}|}}{(1+|\sigma_{i}|)^{1+|\sigma_{i}|}},

where σi=∑j∈Cibj\sigma_{i}=\sum_{j\in C_{i}}b_{j}. Now send 𝒌→∞\bm{k}\to\infty, similar to the proof of Corollary 4.12. ∎

Lastly, we find a capacity bound for the cardinalities of fibers of TU matrices with nonnegative partial row sums.

Corollary 4.14.

Suppose MM is an m×nm\times n TU matrix satisfying 𝐬i≥𝟎\bm{s}_{i}\geq\bm{0} for all i∈[m]i\in[m] (e.g. MM only has 0,1 entries). Assume further that MM does not have an all zero column. Then:

BM​(𝒃)≥cap𝒃⁡(PM)⋅[∏i=1m−1|σi||σi|(1+|σi|)1+|σi|]2⋅|σm||σm|(1+|σm|)1+|σm|.B_{M}(\bm{b})\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M})\cdot\left[\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\frac{|\sigma_{i}|^{|\sigma_{i}|}}{(1+|\sigma_{i}|)^{1+|\sigma_{i}|}}\right]^{2}\cdot\frac{|\sigma_{m}|^{|\sigma_{m}|}}{(1+|\sigma_{m}|)^{1+|\sigma_{m}|}}.

Let A=[M−J​M]A=\begin{bmatrix}M\\ -JM\end{bmatrix}, where JJ has 11s in the anti-diagonal and is zero everywhere else (that is, for any matrix BB with proper dimensions, J​BJB reverses the order of the rows of BB). AA is TU and satisfies the assumptions of Corollary 4.12. So by this corollary:

cap(𝒃,−J​𝒃)(PA)=infxi>0​∀i∈[2​m]PM(xix2​m+1−i:i∈[m])∏i∈[m](xix2​m+1−i)bi=cap𝒃(PM).\cpc_{(\bm{b},-J\bm{b})}(P_{A})=\inf_{x_{i}>0\forall i\in[2m]}\frac{P_{M}\left(\frac{x_{i}}{x_{2m+1-i}}:i\in[m]\right)}{\prod_{i\in[m]}\left(\frac{x_{i}}{x_{2m+1-i}}\right)^{b_{i}}}=\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M}).

We conclude:

BM​(𝒃)≥cap𝒃⁡(PM)⋅[∏i=1m−1|σi||σi|(1+|σi|)1+|σi|]2⋅|σm||σm|(1+|σm|)1+|σm|.B_{M}(\bm{b})\geq\cpc_{\bm{b}}(P_{M})\cdot\left[\prod_{i=1}^{m-1}\frac{|\sigma_{i}|^{|\sigma_{i}|}}{(1+|\sigma_{i}|)^{1+|\sigma_{i}|}}\right]^{2}\cdot\frac{|\sigma_{m}|^{|\sigma_{m}|}}{(1+|\sigma_{m}|)^{1+|\sigma_{m}|}}.

5 Efficiency of Approximation

We prove the algorithmic assertion of Theorem 1.3 using the interiority and ellipsoid argument of [41] (see Sections 5,6 of the arXiv version). We verify the necessary bounds directly for our Laurent polynomials, rather than applying their statements for 0/10/1 configurations verbatim. Throughout this section we assume MM is full row-rank, but this is without loss of generality since one can always remove linearly dependent rows of MM without changing the lattice point counts or the value of the capacity (up to consistency of 𝒃\bm{b}).

Let M∈ℤm×nM\in\mathbb{Z}^{m\times n} be TU with columns 𝒂1,…,𝒂n\bm{a}_{1},\ldots,\bm{a}_{n}, let 𝒃∈ℤm\bm{b}\in\mathbb{Z}^{m} and 𝒌∈ℤ≥0n\bm{k}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{n}, and write

p⁡(𝒙)=PM,𝒌​(𝒙)=∏j=1n∑ℓ=0kjxℓ​𝒂j,ℰ=cap𝒃⁡(p).p(\bm{x})=P_{M,\bm{k}}(\bm{x})=\prod_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{\ell=0}^{k_{j}}x^{\ell\bm{a}_{j}},\qquad\mathcal{E}=\cpc_{\bm{b}}(p).

We show that a deterministic algorithm can approximate log⁡ℰ\log\mathcal{E} to additive error 2−q2^{-q} in time polynomial in

m,n,q=log⁡1ϵ,log⁡(1+‖𝒃‖∞),log⁡(1+‖𝒌‖∞),m,\quad n,\quad q=\log\frac{1}{\epsilon},\quad\log(1+\|\bm{b}\|_{\infty}),\quad\log(1+\|\bm{k}\|_{\infty}),

as long as ℰ≠0\mathcal{E}\neq 0. All inputs are binary encoded and running time is measured in bit operations.

Finally, for Theorem 1.3, set K=‖𝒃‖1K=\|\bm{b}\|_{1} and kj=Kk_{j}=K before performing any reductions. This gives the stated dependence on log⁡(1+‖𝒃‖1)\log(1+\|\bm{b}\|_{1}).

Reduction to 𝒃\bm{b} in the interior.

The Newton polytope of pp is the zonotope Z=M⁡[𝟎,𝒌]Z=M[\bm{0},\bm{k}]; i.e. the sum of the line segments defined by kj​𝒂jk_{j}\bm{a}_{j} for j∈[n]j\in[n].

Let FF be the smallest face of ZZ containing 𝒃\bm{b}. Minimizing and maximizing each coordinate over Q={𝒚∈ℝn:M𝒚=𝒃, 0≤𝒚≤𝒌}Q=\{\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:M\bm{y}=\bm{b},\ \bm{0}\leq\bm{y}\leq\bm{k}\} identifies the set of coordinates forced to equal either 00 and kjk_{j}. Thus we can remove these columns of M,𝒌M,\bm{k} to obtain M′,𝒌′M^{\prime},\bm{k}^{\prime}, and up to translation the zonotope M′​[𝟎,𝒌′]M^{\prime}[\bm{0},\bm{k}^{\prime}] is equal to FF. Restricting to FF and the associated variables preserves the corresponding coefficient and the value of the capacity by a standard optimization argument. Additionally, 𝒃\bm{b} is in the relative interior of the Newton polytope of the new polynomial, up to the same translation between M′​[𝟎,𝒌′]M^{\prime}[\bm{0},\bm{k}^{\prime}] and FF. Thus we may WLOG assume that 𝒃\bm{b} is in the interior of ZZ.

Finally, note that this removal of columns may decrease the rank of MM. Thus, we again remove linearly dependent rows of MM at this point to account for this.

Bounding box for the minimizer.

By Lemma 5.1 (see below), each facet inequality of ZZ can be written with normal 𝒖\bm{u} as

𝒖⊤​𝒚≤h,𝒖∈{0,+1,−1}m,h∈ℤ.\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{y}\leq h,\quad\bm{u}\in\{0,+1,-1\}^{m},\quad h\in\mathbb{Z}.

Since 𝒃\bm{b} is in the interior of ZZ, its slack in each inequality is at least one. Consequently,

B2​(𝒃,1m)⊆Z.B_{2}\left(\bm{b},\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\right)\subseteq Z.

Now set Φ⁡(𝒛)=log⁡p⁡(e𝒛)−𝒃⊤​𝒛\Phi(\bm{z})=\log p(e^{\bm{z}})-\bm{b}^{\top}\bm{z}, noting that log⁡cap𝒃⁡(p)=inf𝒛∈ℝmΦ⁡(𝒛)\log\cpc_{\bm{b}}(p)=\inf_{\bm{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}}\Phi(\bm{z}). Every nonzero coefficient of pp is a positive integer, and so

Φ⁡(𝒛)≥max𝜶∈Z⁡(𝜶−𝒃)⊤​𝒛≥‖𝒛‖2m.\Phi(\bm{z})\geq\max_{\bm{\alpha}\in Z}(\bm{\alpha}-\bm{b})^{\top}\bm{z}\geq\frac{\|\bm{z}\|_{2}}{\sqrt{m}}.

Thus Φ\Phi attains its minimum on ℝm\mathbb{R}^{m}, and every minimizer 𝒛∗\bm{z}^{*} satisfies

‖𝒛∗‖2≤m⋅log⁡p⁡(𝟏)=m​∑j=1nlog⁡(kj+1).\|\bm{z}^{*}\|_{2}\leq\sqrt{m}\cdot\log p(\bm{1})=\sqrt{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\log(k_{j}+1).

In particular, we may optimize over [−R,R]m[-R,R]^{m}, where

R=m​∑j=1nlog⁡(kj+1).R=\sqrt{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\log(k_{j}+1).

This is the interiority-based bounding argument of [41], with log⁡p⁡(𝟏)\log p(\mathbf{1}) replacing the logarithm of the number of configurations.

Lemma 5.1.

Let MM be an m×nm\times n totally unimodular matrix of rank mm with columns 𝐚1,…,𝐚n\bm{a}_{1},\ldots,\bm{a}_{n}, fix 𝐤∈ℤ>0n\bm{k}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{n}, and define the zonotope Z=M⁡[𝟎,𝐤]=∑j=1n𝐚j​[0,kj]Z=M[\bm{0},\bm{k}]=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\bm{a}_{j}[0,k_{j}]. Then the normal vectors of the facets of ZZ can be chosen to have entries in {0,+1,−1}\{0,+1,-1\}.

Proof.

Let FF be some facet of ZZ with normal vector 𝒖\bm{u}. By [38], every facet of the zonotope ZZ is parallel to a Minkowski sum of some subset of the segments {𝒂1​[0,k1],…,𝒂n​[0,kn]}\{\bm{a}_{1}[0,k_{1}],\ldots,\bm{a}_{n}[0,k_{n}]\}. Thus FF is parallel to span⁡{𝒂j:𝒖⊤​𝒂j=0}\mathrm{span}\{\bm{a}_{j}:\bm{u}^{\top}\bm{a}_{j}=0\}. WLOG by reindexing let 𝒂1,…,𝒂m−1\bm{a}_{1},\ldots,\bm{a}_{m-1} span the (m−1)(m-1)-dimensional space parallel to FF, and let CC be the m×(m−1)m\times(m-1) submatrix of the corresponding columns of MM, so that 𝒖∈ker⁡C⊤\bm{u}\in\ker C^{\top}. Define vi=(−1)i+1​detCi^v_{i}=(-1)^{i+1}\det C_{\hat{i}} for all i∈[m]i\in[m], where Ci^C_{\hat{i}} is the matrix CC with row ii missing. A straightforward computation shows that 𝒗⊤​𝒂j=0\bm{v}^{\top}\bm{a}_{j}=0 for all j∈[m−1]j\in[m-1] (duplicate a given column of CC and take determinant), and thus ±𝒗\pm\bm{v} can be chosen as the normal vector of FF. Since MM, and thus CC, is TU, this implies the desired result. ∎

Approximate evaluation.

We show that, for rational 𝒛\bm{z} and 0<τ<10<\tau<1, the objective

Φ(𝒛)=−𝒃⊤𝒛+∑j=1nHkj+1(𝒂j⊤𝒛),HN(t)=log∑r=0N−1er​t,\Phi(\bm{z})=-\bm{b}^{\top}\bm{z}+\sum_{j=1}^{n}H_{k_{j}+1}(\bm{a}_{j}^{\top}\bm{z}),\qquad H_{N}(t)=\log\sum_{r=0}^{N-1}e^{rt},

can be evaluated to additive error τ\tau in time polynomial in the input length, the encoding length of 𝒛\bm{z}, and log⁡1τ\log\frac{1}{\tau}. The dot products are computed exactly using rational arithmetic. To evaluate HNH_{N}, use HN​(0)=log⁡NH_{N}(0)=\log N and, for t≠0t\neq 0, the geometric-series identity

HN​(t)=(N−1)​max⁡{t,0}+ℓ⁡(N​|t|)−ℓ⁡(|t|),ℓ⁡(s)=log⁡(1−e−s).H_{N}(t)=(N-1)\max\{t,0\}+\ell(N|t|)-\ell(|t|),\qquad\ell(s)=\log(1-e^{-s}).

This avoids forming exponentials with large positive arguments.

u:=1−e−s≥12​min⁡{s,1}≥2−B−1.u:=1-e^{-s}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\min\{s,1\}\geq 2^{-B-1}.

so returning zero suffices. Otherwise 0<s<q+30<s<q+3.
